articles.summary: Taiwan raising $4 billion to build industrial park in Texas to support US chipmaking supply chain — project to support countless small manufacturers crucial to TSMC, Foxconn supply chain  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
Taiwan is raising at least $4 billion through the Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association to build an industrial park in Texas. According to Bloomberg, the site is designed to support the countless smaller manufacturers that major manufacturers like TSMC and Foxconn rely on.
“We are going to establish a long-term, sustainable supply chain there that can also be joined by American firms and local workers, and not just Taiwanese companies,” Taiwan Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin said.
Major Taiwanese companies are more than capable of spending the billions of dollars needed to set up shop in the U.S. TSMC, for example, has already spent $165 billion to put up its Arizona site, and has committed a further $100 billion to build four more 2nm fabs. However, they also rely on several smaller manufacturers that do not have the financial capability to expand operations into the U.S. independently. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has even recognized some of these companies in a keynote in Taipei earlier this year, nothing the crucial part that these smaller companies play in the global AI supply chain.
Support for these businesses will not be limited to the planned industrial park, too. The Taiwanese government said that it will also offer loan guarantees to the companies that want to operate on the land, plus support them in communicating with local and federal U.S. officials regarding visas, permits, and other documentation.
Taiwan has reportedly secured a piece of land in Texas specifically for this project, but the Ministry of Economic Affairs didn’t give out any details yet, saying that it will elaborate on the project later. It’s also not limiting itself to a single industrial park, with the government saying that it’s planning for “more than one” site that would cost between $2 billion and $4 billion.
While the U.S. government hasn’t commented on Taiwan’s industrial park plan, the planned $4-billion investment would follow the “Taiwan model” that would help its companies invest in America easily and shorten the AI semiconductor supply chain that relies on Taiwanese industry. But even though these companies are primarily focused on meeting the needs of Taiwanese giants like TSMC, Foxconn, and Wistron, American companies are also welcome to work with them. Kung even said that Elon Musk’s Terafab can take advantage of this prospective supply chain, although he also said that they will not transfer their technologies so that he could integrate them vertically.

articles.full_text:
Intel has confirmed that its next-generation Razor Lake-AX SoCs will launch in 2028, bringing increased AI capabilities.
Intel SVP Confirms Nova Lake For 2027 & Razor Lake For 2028 - AX SoCs Drive AI TOPS To 700
During the "Semiconductors Powering Humanoids" seminar in South Korea's Samseong-dong, Intel SVP Cho Min-sung confirmed the next-generation Nova Lake and Razor Lake SoCs. These SoCs will be arriving in 2027 and 2028, respectively.
The Intel Nova Lake CPUs have been expected for a while, and we have a fair bit of information that is covered in previous articles. But Intel naming Razor Lake this year was definitely a surprise. The company head outlined the performance aspects of the chip, which look impressive.
"We plan to provide performance at the 700 TOPS level with the next-generation Nova Lake early next year and Razer Lake AX in 2028."
Cho Min-Sung (Intel SVP) via The Elec
Min-sung said that Intel's Razor Lake-AX SoCs will offer 700 TOPS of AI compute, an increase of 3.88x over the existing Panther Lake "Core Series 3" chips, which offer 180 TOPS. The Intel Razor Lake-AX SoCs aren't going to be a traditional computing platform. It will be similar to AMD's Ryzen Halo platform, offering several cores, massive GPUs, and increased memory capabilities. The chip will be aimed at premium devices, and one of the markets it will tackle is Physical AI.
Intel stated that Razor Lake-AX's 700 TOPS will far exceed the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin platform, which offers 275 TOPS. That's a 2.5x increase in AI compute. NVIDIA recently released updated versions of its Jetson SoCs, which scale from 160 to 275 TOPS in the mainstream segment. These platforms feature 8 GB and up to 64 GB of VRAM. The Jetson Thor T2000 platform offers around 400 TFLOPS while the T3000 offers 865 TFLOPS of FP4 AI compute. These chips are rated at 40W and 70W, respectively.
Having a large memory pool is essential for AI, so Intel is likely going to have a unified and large pool available on Razor Lake-AX SoCs. These SoCs are expected to feature on-package memory, which will be a return to MoP design first featured on Lunar Lake "Core Series 2" SoCs a few years back.
As the industry doubles down on AI, Physical and Agentic AI-specific chips are becoming the new standard. We have seen NVIDIA venture into the PC space with its latest RTX Spark SoCs, & AMD has been offering Ryzen AI MAX+ Halo chips for a while. Intel creating its own SoC and focusing on the Agentic/Physical AI space is further going to accelerate these segments. Intel's Panther Lake is already a potent solution in the Physical AI space, & Nova Lake/Razor Lake are only going to take them further in this growing market.

While we see multiple reports indicating the discontinuation of the flagship Blackwell GeForce GPU, NVIDIA, on the other hand, denies such reports.
NVIDIA's Jeff Fisher Says RTX 5090 isn't Discontinued After Acknowledging Supply Constraints
Multiple Taiwanese publications have reported NVIDIA's refutation of reports that the RTX 5090 is being discontinued. If you have been following us, you must be aware that a few days ago, there were reports suggesting NVIDIA has ended the supply of the GeForce RTX 5090, the flagship Blackwell GeForce GPU, as it aims to supply the GB202 die for the RTX PRO series.
The reports suggest that NVIDIA will replace the RTX 5090 with the RTX 5080 24 GB as the new flagship RTX 50 series GPU. However, NVIDIA didn't comment on these reports until now, when NVIDIA's senior vice president refuted the rumors. NVIDIA's SVP, Jeff Fisher, reportedly told the Taiwanese media that the reports about the RTX 5090 discontinuation aren't true and that the GPU remains an extremely important core product.
Moreover, he said that the RTX 5090 will continue to ship, refuting the EOL reports. However, Jeff also acknowledged that there are severe supply constraints. The statement appears to highlight the worsening availability of the RTX 5090, which has already reached $5000+ in most regions.
Jeff's statement about the RTX 5090 supply was quoted by 4Gamers and CNA (Taiwanese Central News Agency). The same was published by SJTV (Shin Ji Satellite TV).
As per the reports, Jeff Fisher came to Taiwan to attend the RTX Spark Launch party in Taipei, where he gave his remarks on the RTX 5090 rumors. Jeff reportedly also highlighted the importance of NVIDIA's Gaming and GeForce business and said that there would be no NVIDIA today without this segment.
If what Jeff said regarding the RTX 5090 is true, then we need answers as to why the RTX 5090 suddenly disappeared from NVIDIA's marketplace.
Also, major retailers such as Micro Center removed the GPU from their shelves. Is it that NVIDIA is suddenly resuming production due to backlash? Or was there really a disruption in the supply chain due to shortages? I think we will know soon.

articles.title: Nvidia's RTX Spark Event in San Francisco Attracts Long Lines, But Few Buyers - PCMag
articles.summary: Nvidia's RTX Spark Event in San Francisco Attracts Long Lines, But Few Buyers  PCMagRTX Spark Ignites Global Celebration as New Windows PCs Arrive  NVIDIA BlogNvidia RTX Spark Gaming Tests: Are These New AI Laptops Good for Play, Too?  PCMagBenchmarked: Nvidia's RTX Spark notebook delivers serious local AI compute, at a price  The RegisterNVIDIA RTX Spark PCs Available Today—A New Beginning for Windows PCs  TechPowerUp
articles.full_text:
The Best Buy in San Francisco is no stranger to long customer lines for Nvidia products. That happened again on Friday morning when dozens of people lined up to attend the only official launch “celebration” in the US for Nvidia’s RTX Spark laptops.
PCMag was on the scene, where a line of over 100 consumers wrapped around the store and extended down the building’s side, minutes before the event kicked off at 10 a.m. The sight was reminiscent of the huge crowds for Nvidia’s RTX 3000 graphics card series back in 2021.
This time, though, the crowd wasn’t dead set on purchasing Nvidia’s products. Instead, many people came out of curiosity or because of the free "swag." That’s because the RTX Spark isn’t a graphics card, but the company’s first effort to create Windows laptops built with Nvidia’s Arm-based CPUs, making the products new and untested.
So, while the line was long, it looked like only a handful of people actually bought an RTX Spark model. The machines start at $2,599, far more than a typical laptop. Some customers told us they came merely to try out the RTX Spark before deciding whether to buy it. A few even bluntly said the laptops are too expensive, or joked that PCMag should buy them one.
“I got no money,” said George Gonzalez, a college student who drove over from San Jose, about an hour away, and arrived at about 6 a.m. He was first in line and said, “I love Nvidia. I have a special place for tech in my heart.” But while he can’t afford one now, Gonzalez took a longer-term view, saying he hopes the company will one day create a more affordable RTX Spark laptop that can also run Linux rather than Windows.
“Maybe one day, possibly in the future, they’ll get rid of GPUs entirely, and it’ll just be this [an RTX Spark], but it’ll run better than a GPU. It’ll be the ultimate computer,” he said.
Second in line was Kevin Barreto, who lives near the Best Buy store, and actually came to meet YouTuber iJustine, who was greeting fans at the event. “I like [the RTX Spark]; I kind of want to buy one. But I’m not going to buy one today because of money,” he said with a laugh. “But it’s definitely something on my radar.”
The AI-driven memory shortage, expected to persist over the next two years or longer, is bound to keep RTX Spark pricing high in the short term. Still, the event did start off with a bang when Best Buy employees celebrated the first person to purchase an actual RTX Spark from the store. Sigil Wen, an AI developer who’s partnered with Nvidia to create AI that runs locally on a laptop, proudly held up his HP OmniBook Ultra.
“Why should I pay for my [AI] cloud subscription when I could literally just buy an RTX Spark, and it runs it super fast,” said Wen, the developer of Underdog.AI. “Basically, it’s free ChatGPT.”
“I could cancel all of my subscriptions. I don’t want to send my data to all the data centers,” he added. “I would rather it be private and personal, and on-device.”
That’s perhaps the major selling point of Nvidia’s RTX Spark. Although the laptops are pricey, they also have high-capacity memory, allowing them to run large AI models locally and privately, giving customers an alternative to OpenAI or Anthropic.
“There’s a high price on multiple Nvidia products. But for the amount of product you are getting in comparison to anything else on the market, I think it’s fair for what it is,” said another interested customer named George T, who already owns an Nvidia RTX 5080 GPU.
At the event, Nvidia held several demo stations to show off the laptop's capabilities, including how they run games with the photorealistic graphics from DLSS 5. “It looked really cool, the NBA game,” said one attendee named Sherry. But on the price, she noted: “It’s pretty expensive. That’s why I’m looking at it and learning more about it before purchasing.”
Many also attended because Nvidia reached out to them with an email, possibly because they had signed up to receive marketing emails from the company. Meanwhile, one woman told us she was there because her husband, a computer scientist, was interested in the product.
The whole crowd also seemed to linger, hoping to win a free RTX Spark laptop signed by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. At one point, Huang briefly appeared on a smartphone at the event. But once the five raffle winners were announced, many attendees exited the store.

articles.title: Why India’s Multi-Fuel Future Needs Intelligent Infrastructure - Autocar Professional
articles.summary: Why India’s Multi-Fuel Future Needs Intelligent Infrastructure  Autocar Professional
articles.full_text:
India’s transition to cleaner mobility is likely to involve petrol, diesel, CNG and electric power running in parallel, creating a need for integrated digital infrastructure that helps drivers and fleet operators plan refuelling and charging.
India’s energy transition is often described as a race towards a single winner. Petrol gives way to CNG, CNG gives way to electric, and electric eventually gives way to hydrogen, with older fuels quietly retiring somewhere along the way. It is a clean story. It is also not the story that is actually unfolding on Indian roads.
Walk into any fuel station on a major highway today and you will find petrol, diesel and CNG dispensers standing side by side, often with an EV charging point added more recently. Talk to a fleet operator and you will find vehicles running on diesel, CNG and electricity within the same fleet, sometimes on the same route. India is not transitioning from one fuel to another in a straight line. It is settling, for the foreseeable future, into a multi-fuel economy where several energy sources operate in parallel, each suited to a different vehicle class, geography or use case.
This is not a failure to commit. It is a rational response to India’s scale and diversity. A two-wheeler in a dense city, a long-haul truck crossing three states and a public bus fleet in a tier-two town do not share the same fuel economics, range requirements or refuelling access. Electric makes sense for one. CNG makes more sense for another. Diesel remains, for now, the only workable choice for a third. Pretending that this will resolve into a single fuel within a decade is optimistic in a way that ground reality does not support.
What this multi-fuel reality demands, and mostly does not yet have, is infrastructure that can communicate across fuel types instead of treating each one as an isolated silo.
Today, if you are planning a route, checking CNG availability means using one system, or more often, relying on word of mouth. Checking charging infrastructure means using another. Checking diesel supply at a remote station means calling ahead and hoping. There is no single layer that lets a driver, dispatcher or logistics planner see fuel and energy availability across all these types in one place. Each fuel has effectively built its own information island, and the traveller is left to swim between them.
The cost of this fragmentation is not abstract. A fleet that mixes diesel and CNG vehicles has to operate with two separate mental models for route planning because the data infrastructure behind each fuel type was never designed to communicate with the other. A driver switching from a CNG-run route to one with poor CNG coverage has no early warning system to alert them. This friction has nothing to do with the vehicles themselves and everything to do with the absence of a common, fuel-agnostic layer of information underpinning them.
Intelligent infrastructure, in a multi-fuel context, does not mean picking a favourite fuel and digitising it well. It means building the connective layer that allows petrol, diesel, CNG and electricity to coexist as visible, comparable and plannable options within the same system, on the same map and as part of the same decision a driver makes before starting a journey. It means data infrastructure that is as fuel-agnostic as the vehicle fleets it needs to serve.
The multi-fuel phase of India’s mobility story is not a temporary inconvenience on the way to a cleaner endpoint. For much of the country, it may be the endpoint itself for a long time to come. Treating it that way, and building infrastructure intelligent enough to support it rather than infrastructure that quietly bets on one fuel winning, is the more honest place to start.

articles.title: Understanding Starshield: SpaceX's Military Version of Starlink - IDNFinancials
articles.summary: Understanding Starshield: SpaceX's Military Version of Starlink  IDNFinancials
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — Ukraine stated on Wednesday (10/14) that SpaceX has restricted Starlink services used for military purposes.
These restrictions reportedly hinder Ukraine's drone attack operations and air defense systems.
Cited from Reuters, this issue highlights the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield, a system developed for U.S. military needs.
Elon Musk stated that the two are separate services, although in many ways, both rely on the same satellite technology.
“Starshield is owned and controlled by the U.S. government,” Musk wrote in an X post on Wednesday (10/14).
He added that speed or usage restrictions for Starshield are determined by the U.S. military or the president.
Meanwhile, Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX.
Musk asserted that the service should only be used for civilian or defensive activities, not for offensive military operations.
According to Musk, use for military attacks is not customary for a commercial company.
What is Starlink?
Starlink is a major revenue source for SpaceX. This satellite internet service relies on over 11,000 satellites that transmit internet connections to user receiver devices. These devices are approximately the size of a folded newspaper.
The service has around 1.3 million subscribers, ranging from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines.
Since launching its first Starlink satellite in 2019, SpaceX has continuously expanded its satellite network in low Earth orbit to provide internet services to various regions.
Starlink offers faster connections compared to conventional communication satellites, which generally operate much higher above Earth's surface and are far fewer in number.
At the start of the war, Starlink provided a critical communication advantage for Ukraine and transformed how the military operates on the battlefield.
However, Musk limited the service's use for certain military purposes while developing Starshield, a more secure network for government and military missions.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops satellite systems for the Pentagon's military and intelligence needs.
Starshield was developed by SpaceX to meet the Pentagon's military and intelligence requirements.
Unlike Starlink, which provides commercial internet services, Starshield offers secure communications with stronger encryption and specialized receiver devices.
However, this service still relies on the Starlink satellite network as its primary infrastructure.
According to SpaceX, Starshield leverages the technology, engineering, and operational experience developed through Starlink.
In addition to providing encrypted communication services, Starshield is also designed for Earth observation and to support the use of sensors and other devices on satellites.
The Pentagon, Starshield's largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on Starlink and Starshield services.
The Pentagon has also purchased specialized Starshield satellites, including communication satellites for missile early warning missions and a constellation of spy satellites for the U.S. National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), as reported by Reuters in 2024.
Questions about the relationship between Starlink and Starshield arose after Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022.
SpaceX introduced Starshield that same year. However, because national security space programs are classified, the functional and usage differences between Starlink and Starshield are not fully clear.
The distinction between the two services was also a source of dispute between the Pentagon and SpaceX earlier this year.
Reuters reported that they disagreed over price increases for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict.
SpaceX found that some customers paying approximately US$5,000 per terminal for Starlink should have been using Starshield, which costs about US$25,000 per terminal.
The UK has also used Starshield.
The UK Ministry of Defence told Reuters that the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations, and ground infrastructure as Starlink.
However, Starshield uses its own receiver devices and network gateways, although it still relies on Starlink's satellite infrastructure.
Several other U.S. partners are also evaluating the system.
The New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters that the country is testing Starshield to assess its utility in military operations. (ARF)

Taiwan just announced plans to criminalize AI chip shipments to China, and the legal gap still open is the only thing standing between three major semiconductor companies and a tighter regulatory net.
Until now, someone in Taiwan who shipped a rack of AI servers to a buyer in China faced no direct criminal penalty at home. On October 16, 2026, Taiwan’s Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin confirmed that Taipei plans to add AI servers and cutting-edge semiconductors to its controlled goods list. That would make these shipments a crime under the Foreign Trade Act.
“About to” means the plan has been announced but is still waiting on the law. It needs a legal amendment, and Kung gave no timeline.
For shareholders of NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) and Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI), the effect is mixed. Closing the Taiwan channel could remove gray-market demand that never showed up in official China sales, but it also reduces regulatory risk around all three companies.
Friday’s moves came with a broader chip selloff and had little to do with this news. NVIDIA closed at $214.13, down 1.43%, worth $5.17 trillion. Taiwan Semiconductor fell 2.28% to $412.61, down 8.98% over the past week, and is worth $ 1.89 trillion. Super Micro dropped 9.86% to $31.63, worth $20.78 billion, after a one-week decline of 24.43%.
What Taipei Has Proposed
Taiwan’s current controls rely on a company blacklist that added Huawei and SMIC in mid-2025. The new approach would replace that list with a restriction covering the entire Chinese market.
In remarks reported in translation, Kung said “the measures we take on certain controlled items will correspond with those of the United States,” giving enforcement agencies “more legal tools” against smuggling.
He tied the move to the trade agreement Taiwan signed with Washington on January 15. That deal cut US tariffs on most Taiwanese goods from 20% to 15% and came with $250 billion in Taiwanese company commitments for US projects. Separately, DPP legislator Chung Chia-pin has drafted an amendment that adds a mainland China semiconductor clause, and it still has to pass.
The channel through which restricted hardware entered China was simple: servers built in or routed through Taiwan and other hubs ended up with Chinese buyers. Taiwan detained alleged AI chip smugglers in May.
In July, prosecutors pursued Super Micro executives on forgery charges. No one has been charged with chip smuggling in that case.
Why Super Micro Carries the Most Exposure
NVIDIA has already removed China from its numbers. Its third-quarter fiscal 2027 outlook of $108.0 billion excludes all China data center compute revenue, so lost gray-market demand would not hurt its guidance, and closer alignment with Washington could help when future licenses come up.
Taiwan Semiconductor makes the chips but does not ship servers. Its main gain is stability in the trade deal that sets its home market’s tariff rate.
Super Micro builds systems in Taiwan, and its board has disclosed an independent review of certain transactions related to export-control issues. That makes it the most exposed and most volatile of the three.
Regardless, Kung gave no start date, penalty schedule, or final list of covered products. Smuggling enforcement had already been a US and Singapore story, so Taiwan’s step adds to existing efforts, and the market appeared to treat it that way.
What the Taiwan Rule Means for NVIDIA’s Outlook
NVIDIA looks well positioned. The Taiwan rule cuts off demand the company never booked, while revenue grew 105.8% in the last quarter and management called its outlook “supply-constrained.”
At about 43 times earnings, the stock is priced for growth. But the new policy takes risk away from the business and adds none.
Taiwan Semiconductor participates in the AI expansion without server exposure. After a weekly drop of 8.98%, it raised fourth-quarter revenue guidance from $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion.
This view will be tested by whether Chung’s amendment passes Taiwan’s legislature with a start date and by whether NVIDIA’s next earnings report meets its $108.0 billion guidance.

articles.title: Who Owns Starlink? SpaceX, Its Shareholders, and the Spin-Off That Never Came - KeepTrack
articles.summary: Who Owns Starlink? SpaceX, Its Shareholders, and the Spin-Off That Never Came  KeepTrack
articles.full_text:
SpaceX owns Starlink. Starlink is not a separate company with its own shareholders or stock. It is the main business inside SpaceX’s Connectivity segment, so whoever owns SpaceX owns Starlink. That means Elon Musk, who controls about 82% of SpaceX’s votes (84.4% counting his unexercised options), plus Alphabet, early investors, employees, and anyone who has bought SpaceX’s Class A shares on the Nasdaq under the ticker SPCX since June 12, 2026. Starlink had 12.0 million subscribers at June 30, 2026, and the KeepTrack catalog counts 11,131 Starlink satellites in orbit as of October 2026.
The rest of this page covers how the ownership is structured, what the filings say Starlink earns, why the long-expected Starlink spin-off did not happen, and how much of the business now comes from government customers through Starshield.
Who owns Starlink?
SpaceX does, directly and entirely. The company’s S-1 and quarterly filings report Starlink as part of one of three operating segments. They are (Falcon, Dragon and Starship), Connectivity (Starlink broadband, Starshield and Starlink Mobile), and AI (xAI, Grok and X, added in the February 2026 merger). No outside investor holds a stake in Starlink by itself.
That makes the ownership question the same as for SpaceX. The June 12, 2026 prospectus lists Musk with 93.6% of the ten-vote Class B stock and 84.4% of combined voting power after the offering, figures that count 350 million Class B shares underlying his options. Without them, the prospectus puts his voting power at about 82.4%. Alphabet’s second-quarter 10-Q valued its SpaceX shares at $94.1 billion as of June 30, 2026. Public shareholders own Class A stock with one vote per share. Who owns SpaceX has the full shareholder list.
Starlink does operate through subsidiaries in many of the countries it serves, which is why a Dutch Starlink entity’s annual accounts were, for years, one of the few official financial documents outsiders could read. Those subsidiaries belong to SpaceX.
How Starlink ended up inside SpaceX
Starlink was never set up as a separate venture. SpaceX funded it from its own balance sheet, and outside money came in at the SpaceX level. The clearest example is the January 2015 round, when Google and Fidelity put $1 billion into SpaceX as the company was beginning work on a satellite internet network. NPR reported at the time that the two investors would own just under 10% of SpaceX together. Alphabet’s stake is now one of the largest disclosed indirect positions in Starlink, because it owns SpaceX.
The constellation grew from there. The KeepTrack catalog records 120 Starlink satellites launched in 2019, 1,690 in 2022 and 3,171 in 2025, the largest single year so far. Subscribers followed a few years behind the hardware, from 2.3 million at the end of 2023 to 12.0 million at mid-2026.
Spectrum deals are adding new shareholders for Starlink’s sake. EchoStar agreed in 2025 to sell SpaceX wireless licenses for Starlink Mobile, and SpaceX’s Q2 2026 10-Q says the price includes about $11.1 billion of SpaceX Class A stock, roughly 261.8 million shares. The 10-Q says those shares will be issued when the deal finally closes, expected around November 2027. EchoStar will then be a SpaceX shareholder because Starlink needed its spectrum, but what it gets is SpaceX stock, not a piece of Starlink.
Can you buy Starlink stock?
Not as a separate stock. The only way to own Starlink on an exchange is to buy SPCX, which closed at $162.57 on October 9, 2026. That share also carries the launch business and the AI segment, which lost $1.26 billion at the operating line in the second quarter of 2026 while Connectivity earned $1.66 billion. Our guide to buying SpaceX stock covers the ticker and the indirect routes.
Watch for “Starlink stock” offers outside a brokerage. Since Starlink has no shares of its own, any pitch selling pre-IPO Starlink stock is selling something other than what it claims.
How much money does Starlink make?
Starlink is the profitable core of . In 2025, Connectivity revenue was $11.39 billion, 61% of SpaceX’s $18.67 billion total, and the segment earned $4.42 billion of operating income while the other two segments lost money. The S-1 says consumer subscriptions made up more than 60% of Connectivity revenue in 2025.
| Period | Revenue | Operating income | Subscribers (period end) | ARPU per month | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | $3.87B | $0.47B | 2.3M | $99 | 
| 2024 | $7.60B | $2.01B | 4.4M | $91 | 
| 2025 | $11.39B | $4.42B | 8.9M | $81 | 
| Q1 2026 | $3.26B | $1.19B | 10.3M | $66 | 
| Q2 2026 | $4.29B | $1.66B | 12.0M | $66 | 
Two trends run in opposite directions. Subscribers roughly doubled each year, and revenue followed. Average revenue per user fell from $99 a month in 2023 to $66 in 2026 as Starlink expanded into lower-priced markets. The S-1 counted 164 countries, territories and other markets served as of March 31, 2026.
The second quarter of 2026 showed the mix shifting toward larger customers. Consumer revenue was $2.49 billion, up 44% from a year earlier. Enterprise and government revenue was $1.81 billion, up 108%, as airline, business and government contracts grew. SpaceX said in the Q2 release that it signed a major agreement with American Airlines and activated service on Southwest, Virgin Atlantic, Iberia and Aer Lingus.
How many Starlink satellites are there?
The KeepTrack catalog shows 11,131 Starlink satellites in orbit as of October 2026, with 12,918 launched since 2019 and 1,787 already reentered. SpaceX launched 3,171 Starlink satellites in 2025 and 2,167 more so far in 2026, by the catalog’s count. SpaceX’s own S-1 described “approximately 9,600 Starlink broadband and mobile satellites” as of March 31, 2026, a count of satellites in service rather than every object still in orbit.
You can watch the constellation grow on the Starlink satellite count page or explore it in 3D on the Starlink constellation hub.
Starshield and government customers
Starshield is the government version of the network. The S-1 describes it as “a secure satellite network designed specifically for government customers and national security applications,” and SpaceX books its revenue in the Connectivity segment under long-term government contracts.
The money has grown fast. The Q2 2026 release says SpaceX was “awarded over $6 billion in multi-year U.S. government contracts for Starshield,” primarily from two Force contracts for low Earth orbit communications and sensing constellations. Reporting at the time identified two large May 2026 awards that match that description, a $2.29 billion agreement for the Space Data Network backbone, reported by SpaceNews, and a $4.16 billion first increment of the space-based airborne moving target indicator program, reported by Breaking Defense. SpaceX did not itemize the awards in its release.
The count above includes only catalog objects named STARLINK, so government satellites built on Starshield designs are not in it. The national security work also means part of Starlink’s revenue depends on the U.S. government budget, while the consumer side depends on households in more than 160 markets.
Will Starlink be spun off or have its own IPO?
For years, the expected path was a Starlink IPO. Analysts assumed SpaceX would separate the cash-generating internet business from the capital-hungry rocket program and list it on its own. That did not happen. SpaceX instead merged with xAI in February 2026 and listed the combined company in June, with Starlink inside it.
As of October 11, 2026, SpaceX had not announced any plan to spin off or separately list Starlink, and its Q2 2026 earnings release does not mention one. A spin-off would require a decision by a board that Musk controls through his voting power, so it is his call.
What comes next for Starlink
The next growth leg is Starlink Mobile, the direct-to-cell service. SpaceX’s Q2 release says the FCC approved the transfer of EchoStar licenses covering 65 MHz of U.S. spectrum, part of a deal SpaceX is paying for partly in stock. On October 8, 2026, SpaceX agreed to buy Grain Management’s nationwide 800 MHz holdings for Starlink Mobile, pending FCC approval. The release also lists new Starlink Mobile partners SoftBank, NTT Docomo and Spark NZ.
Starship matters too. Flight 13 in July 2026 deployed 20 production Starlink V3 satellites, according to SpaceX’s Q2 release. If Starship flies often, each launch can add much more capacity than a Falcon 9 load, which is the main lever on Starlink’s cost per subscriber.
Frequently asked questions
Who owns Starlink?
SpaceX owns Starlink entirely, as part of its Connectivity segment. SpaceX's largest owner is Elon Musk, who held about 82% of the voting power after the June 2026 IPO (84.4% counting his options), and its Class A shares trade on the Nasdaq as SPCX.
Does Elon Musk own Starlink?
Indirectly. Musk controls SpaceX, which owns Starlink, through his super-voting Class B stock, 93.6% of that class counting his options, per the June 2026 prospectus.
Is there a Starlink IPO?
No. As of October 2026, SpaceX had not announced a Starlink spin-off or separate listing, and Starlink is included in SPCX shares. SpaceX listed the whole company on June 12, 2026 instead.
How many Starlink subscribers are there?
SpaceX reported 12.0 million Starlink subscribers at June 30, 2026, double the 6.0 million of a year earlier. Average revenue per user was $66 a month that quarter.
How much revenue does Starlink make?
SpaceX's Connectivity segment, which is mostly Starlink, earned $11.39 billion of revenue and $4.42 billion of operating income in 2025. In Q2 2026 it brought in $4.29 billion of revenue and $1.66 billion of operating income.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is SpaceX's secure satellite network for U.S. government and national security customers, reported inside the Connectivity segment. SpaceX said it won more than $6 billion of multi-year Starshield contracts in Q2 2026.

articles.title: Why Canadian Starlink subscribers (probably) shouldn't worry about U.S interference - Yahoo News Canada
articles.summary: Why Canadian Starlink subscribers (probably) shouldn't worry about U.S interference  Yahoo News Canada
articles.full_text:
Earlier this week, Ukrainian officials said they had lost some access to Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, the satellite communications system operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX.
Musk, CEO of SpaceX, denied any involvement in restricting Ukraine's access, saying that decision would be up to the U.S. government.
Meanwhile, on Friday, U.S. President Donald Trump denied he was involved in the decision to restrict access and said he didn't think Musk was involved either.
Trump's remarks followed a Reuters report that the White House had ordered the restrictions.
Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink terminals stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance over Ukrainian territory.
Still, the potential ability of the U.S government to affect the operation of a Starlink-related satellite system may also have raised questions about Washington's ability to influence commercial users of the system.
In Canada, for example, Starlink provides internet access in remote areas and has about 500,000 users.
Here's a look at the U.S. government's relationship with Starlink and Starshield, and the role it plays in each.
What's the difference between Starlink and Starshield?
Starlink is a Space X's commercial satellite internet network, with more than 11,000 satellites and roughly 13 million subscribers. It is available to businesses and individuals.
Its low-Earth-orbit satellites allow it to deliver faster connections than traditional satellite internet systems.
The network gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how its military operates on the battlefield.
But when Musk and SpaceX became concerned about the commercial system being used for military purposes, the company created Starshield, said Mark Hilborne, an associate professor in the defence studies department at King's College London.
Unlike the thousands of satellites used in the Starlink network, Starshield is limited to around 250, Hilborne said.
It's also a more secure network, is not publicly available and is used specifically for government and military purposes. Its secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals.
Few countries have access to Starshield, Hillborne said. The U.S. is the main customer, while the United Kingdom and Ukraine also have access. In Ukraine's case, the Pentagon covers the fees and allows the country to use the system.
While Starshield's missions are separate from Starlink's commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield's secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
What role does the U.S. government have in Starshield?
According to Musk, the Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S government. That means any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and, ultimately, by the president, he said.
"Mostly, it is used by [the U.S.] and it's for them. And so they probably make the ultimate decisions" regarding its use, Hilborne said.
According to a 2024 Reuters report, the Pentagon has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office.
But the relationship between Starshield and the U.S. government is "fuzzy," Craig Douglas Albert, a political science professor and graduate director of the Intelligence, Defense and Cybersecurity program at Augusta University in Georgia, said in an email to CBC News.
SpaceX develops and supplies Starshield through government contracts, meaning the system is privately owned but procured by the U.S. government, Albert said.
"There is a lot on this relationship that is classified and thus, the direct relationship is still unclear," he said.
Does the U.S. government have any control over Starlink?
Again, Albert says, it's not entirely clear.
The U.S can regulate Starlink through licensing requirements and the terms of government contracts governing how the company operates, he said.
However, much of the relationship is classified, limiting public understanding of how much influence the U.S. government has over Starlink, Albert said.
But the U.S. has no direct control over Starlink itself, he said.
What major satellite systems does the U.S. government control?
Major examples would include the Global Positioning System (GPS), a space-based radio-navigation system owned by the U.S. government and operated by the United States Space Force. Its satellites provide services to civilian and military users.
The U.S. Space Force also operates Wideband Global SATCOM (WGS) and Advanced Extremely High Frequency (AEHF) system for military communications, as well as the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) for advanced missile warning.
"The relationship between satellite technology and the U.S. government exists from everyday consumer and citizen consumption through advanced national security operations," Albert said.
Should Canadians be concerned about U.S. government control over private commercial systems?
Hilborne said that while the U.S. may technically have the capability to turn off such a system in a region of Canada, for example, such a move would likely be resisted by commercial operators.
However, the U.S. government could likely apply leverage to a company like SpaceX to bend to its wishes, he suggested.
Albert added that citizens "should always force accountability of technology that is dual use and has a relationship between citizen consumer consumption and national security."

articles.full_text:
Starlink has said it has worked with Indian regulators, industry, and operators for over five years and built dedicated infrastructure in the country with requisite government approvals, asserting its readiness to provide high-speed internet services in India amid the ongoing satcom row. In a post on X, the Elon Musk-led company said, “We have worked closely with regulators, industry and operators in India for 5+ years, and built a network of dedicated systems, gateways, and other infrastructure all in-country to exclusively serve Indian traffic safely and securely — and all with the requisite government approvals.”
Starlink’s statement comes after Reliance Industries said it welcomes competition in satellite communications, including Starlink, while asserting that every player must abide by the law and rules of the land. The company’s remarks come amid a public spat between Musk and Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani, with Musk alleging that “certain oligarchs” were blocking Starlink’s entry into India to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people.
The Ministry of Communications has maintained that the satellite communications authorisation framework is fair and non-discriminatory, with Starlink, Reliance Jio’s satellite business, and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb broadly at the same regulatory stage, with mandatory security assessments still to be completed before spectrum can be assigned. Communications Minister Jyotiraditya Scindia has reiterated that India does not permit monopolies and that commercial operations can begin only after the necessary security requirements are met and spectrum charges are finalised.
Starlink has obtained GMPCS licences and IN-SPACe authorisation, and has signed memorandums of understanding with Airtel and Jio, but is still awaiting final security and spectrum-related approvals before commencing commercial services. The company has already built its ground infrastructure in India, comprising 20 gateway sites with hundreds of antennas, with the company’s Vice-President of Starlink Business Operations at SpaceX, Lauren Dreyer, stating that the company designed its India set-up around local security requirements and regulations.
The satcom row highlights the challenges facing Starlink as it seeks approval to enter India, where commercial competition, government security requirements, and restrictions on internet access intersect. The government’s rejection of Musk’s allegations and its insistence on a fair and non-discriminatory framework is expected to shape the future of the satellite communications sector in the country.

articles.title: What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military version of Starlink? - Defense News
articles.summary: What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military version of Starlink?  Defense News
articles.full_text:
Ukraine said on Wednesday that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses.
The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon.
While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military or the president. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
WHAT IS STARLINK?
Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX, is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
WHAT IS STARSHIELD?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarized version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programs has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported.
SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal.
Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s defense ministry has told Reuters.
Other U.S. partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.

articles.title: Satellites to outnumber visible stars, astronomers warn - AOL.com
articles.summary: Satellites to outnumber visible stars, astronomers warn  AOL.com
articles.full_text:
Astronomers have warned satellites could outnumber visible stars in the night sky as applications for more than two million satellites are being considered.
A meeting organised by the Royal Astronomical Society (RAS) in London heard how the rapid spread of space technology will soon “change the night sky for everyone”.
On a very clear night it is possible to see around 4,500 stars, but moving dots of light created by spacecraft as they reflect the sun will soon surpass that, experts predict, destroying dark, quiet skies for amateur stargazers and professional astronomers.
If all the planned satellites are launched there would be 15 times as many visible satellites in the night sky as stars.
SpaceX alone has had permission to launch one million orbital data centre satellites in the coming years, which could be 500ft wide for its Starmind constellation.
“This will be a vast constellation, and this would really get us into the regime of visible satellites outnumbering the visible stars,” said Dr Jonathan McDowell, honorary professor at Durham University.
“A variety of companies and organisations have total requests for over two million satellites.
“If they’re at 500 kilometres high, they’re a problem for the average person looking at the night sky, you’ll see these things all over the horizon.
“Satellites that are 1000 kilometers or so, like the Chinese constellations, they’re going to be a real problem for professional astronomers because they’ll be illuminated throughout the night. It’s going to be dramatically bad.”
There are nearly 17,000 satellites in orbit, with SpaceX’s Starlink constellation alone accounting for 11,000. Amazon Leo is planning to increase its satellites ten-fold to have more than 3,000, while various Chinese constellation providers have filed applications for 200,000 spacecraft.
US-based StarCloud has submitted a proposal to the Federal Communications Commission for an 88,000-satellite data-centre constellation, while Cowboy Space, another US firm, wants to launch 20,000 satellites for its planned orbital AI data grid.
Space hardware will inundate night sky
Dr McDowell calculated how many illuminated satellites might be visible during the night if all the proposed constellations were sent into orbit and found that in midsummer at midnight there could be as many as 70,000 satellites visible in the night sky – half from Starmind.
Britain would be particularly affected because many satellites are in a high-inclination orbit, meaning they pass overhead rather than close to the horizon, and so are more visible.
Advertisement
The Royal Astronomical Society said the world was at a “critical point” where the proliferation of satellites was about to “change the sky and pose an existential threat to astronomy” because the reflected sunlight leaves bright streaks across astronomical images.
Dr Robert Massey, deputy executive director of the Royal Astronomical Society, said: “We’ve been backing astronomy since 1820, and we’ve been involved in preserving dark and quiet skies from the start of that effort.
“And I don’t mean 2019, which is when the first batch of Starlink satellites launched, I actually mean 1961 when there was a prior furore about the launch of something called Project West Ford, which was the US effort to deploy a kind of backup communication system of millions of copper needles, copper dipoles, to reflect radio waves back to Earth in the event of a war.
“The RAS joined the Soviet Union and astronomers around the world in different countries in condemning it and saying it would shut off the sky to their nascent science of radio astronomy. So we’ve sort of been here before.
“What’s interesting about that time is there were some public protests as well, which seemed extraordinary. And I’d like the public to be a bit more engaged with this issue as well.”
Dr René Tronsgaard, of the University of Cambridge, warned that the bright trails from satellites were also harming the ability to find Earth-like exoplanets.
Pollution and climate change risks
Experts are concerned that the increased numbers of launches and satellites burning up in the atmosphere at the end of their lives could cause serious atmospheric pollution and exacerbate climate change.
Black carbon released from rockets as well as aluminium products released by ablation during re-entry may also cause depletion of the ozone layer.
Prof Eloise Marais, of University College London, said: “The impacts of rockets and re-entries on the ozone layer and climate is so far very small in comparison to Earth-bound industrial sources, but this may change.”
The meeting also heard how the reflectivity from space-based data centres and huge orbital mirrors also threatens the circadian rhythms of birds, nocturnal mammals and insects crucial for pollination.
David Rees, of Paradigm Factor, which builds space-based scientific instruments, called for tighter regulation of satellites.
He added: “It will not be easy, given that access to and use of ‘Space’ is no longer entirely controlled by National Agencies, but is operated largely by profit-driven organisations owned by multi-billionaires.”

articles.title: Europe's answer to Starlink: Who is building IRIS² and what is Germany's role - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Europe's answer to Starlink: Who is building IRIS² and what is Germany's role  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
Who controls the satellites on which armies rely? Reports of Starlink limits in Ukraine highlight the question. The EU is building IRIS², a 348-satellite network with a Bremen manufacturer.
This week, the Ukrainian army reported restrictions to the Starlink satellite service. The connection drops as soon as the receivers are travelling at more than 160 kilometres per hour, as is the case with drones.
The service was initially partially restored, but an upper limit remained in place. It is unclear who ordered the restriction.
SpaceX boss Elon Musk rejected responsibility that the company ordered the shutdown. Starshield is under the direct control of the US government, he wrote on X.
It is important to distinguish between the two systems: Starlink and Starshield are both developed by SpaceX but aimed at different customers. Starlink is the service for private and business users, Starshield is designed for governments and the military.
Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski reacted sharply on X, writing: "Hey, Elon Musk, you big man, are you once again playing politics with your products? As your European customers we are keeping a close eye on you."
Poland has paid for a large share of the Ukrainian terminals. This has once again raised the question of how dependent armed forces are on satellite links. Europe has therefore been working for some time on its own solution.
The European answer: IRIS²
The EU has been developing IRIS², its own satellite network, for around six years. The acronym stands for "Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite".
In German this roughly means infrastructure for resilience, connectivity and security via satellites. The system is intended to provide secure connections for governments, companies and citizens and to close mobile coverage gaps in Europe and Africa.
For encryption it will rely on quantum technology via the European quantum communication infrastructure EuroQCI.
In early August, the European Commission and the SpaceRISE consortium agree on the implementation. The network will grow to 348 satellites, 330 in low Earth orbit and 18 in medium Earth orbit.
A further 66 additional satellites are intended specifically to strengthen defence, security and emergency services. According to the Commission’s calculations, this will increase secured capacity for public-sector users by 60 percent in the EU and by 54 percent worldwide.
The focus is on states, the military and critical services; later on, private individuals are also to be able to use the network. The first satellites are scheduled to launch in 2029. Initial services are to be introduced gradually from 2029 or 2030.
Germany's role
Germany is represented by the Bremen-based space company Orbitale Hochtechnologie Bremen (OHB).
On 31 August it signed a contract worth just under €1 billion with satellite operator SES for 18 satellites in medium Earth orbit for IRIS².
A single satellite weighs around 2.6 tonnes at launch. OHB chief executive Marco Fuchs sees the programme as an important step towards greater European independence.
Germany’s share of the project sparked disputes early on.
In December 2023, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs sent a strongly worded letter to the companies involved demanding urgent clarification of the German industry’s participation and its share in value creation, as reported by the Frankfurter Rundschau daily.
Bundeswehr: Its own satellite network?
Independently of IRIS², the Bundeswehr is planning its own satellite network. It is a national project financed by the federal government.
Major General Armin Fleischmann, the Bundeswehr’s space commissioner in the Cyber and Information Domain, told regional public broadcaster MDR that the plan is for a constellation similar to Starlink, only smaller.
He told the Handelsblatt business newspaper they wanted to have "flying Fritzboxes" in space. The network is initially to cover NATO’s eastern flank, under national control. Individual components will come from Western partners, including the United States.
As early as September 2025, defence minister Boris Pistorius announced at the space congress of the Federation of German Industries in Berlin that a total of €35 billion would be invested in military space projects by 2030. In July he visited OHB in Bremen to inspect satellite programmes and ongoing production.
The project is called SATCOMBw 4, short for satellite communication of the Bundeswehr. In its final expansion stage, according to the Bundeswehr, it is to comprise a three-digit number of satellites in low Earth orbit and cost between eight and ten billion euros. An initial partial constellation with up to 40 satellites is scheduled to be operational as early as 2029, with full operations planned from 2030.
The joint venture "OHB Rheinmetall Space Networks", based in Bremen, is bidding for the contract According to company information, OHB would be responsible for the satellites, Rheinmetall for the ground stations and end devices. No decision has yet been taken.
Industry reports suggest that the contract award could come around the turn of the year, though insiders consider early 2027 possible as well. OHB would then be involved in both major projects: in IRIS² as satellite manufacturer and in the Bundeswehr network as part of the joint venture.
Up to now, the Bundeswehr has been using two of its own satellites in geostationary orbit at around 36,000 kilometres altitude, COMSATBw-1 and COMSATBw-2, launched in 2009 and 2010.
Their successors are being built by Airbus and are scheduled to be handed over in orbit in 2029. The first of the three German radar satellites SARah was launched in 2022 on a Falcon 9 rocket from SpaceX.
Young Belgian company helping to build Europe’s satellite network
The satellites for IRIS² are being built by several companies. The largest share will not be supplied by an established group but by a young company:
Aerospacelab, founded in 2018 and based in Charleroi in Belgium, is building 264 satellites for low Earth orbit.
The order volume amounts to €2.4 billion, according to the company. The satellites are to be delivered by 2030. They will be produced in a new factory in Charleroi, where up to 500 satellites per year are to be built from 2027.
Airbus is building at least 66 satellites in the first layer for military communication, which are due to be ready in 2029. This means the entire low-orbit segment with 330 satellites has been allocated.
Together with the 18 OHB satellites for medium orbit, the network will comprise 348 satellites.
How realistic is 2029?
Whether the timetable can be met remains an open question. The first satellites are scheduled to launch in 2029; according to media reports, the original plan was for them to go up two years earlier.
Experts view rocket launches as the bottleneck. Even the best satellites cannot reach space without rockets and those unable to launch them themselves remain dependent on others.
Europe is relying on the Ariane 6 launch vehicle, which has been lifting off into space since 2024. Andreas Knopp of the Bundeswehr University Munich points out in the weekly paper Das Parlament that the number of launches is limited, while political scientist Antje Nötzold of TU Chemnitz speaks in MDR of a "launcher problem."
So far this year, Ariane 6 has launched four times, three of those flights carrying satellites for Amazon Leo into orbit, the US company’s satellite internet service that is also intended to compete with Starlink.
Amazon has booked at least 18 Ariane 6 launches. In early August, the Commission named the procurement of launch services for IRIS² as one of the next steps.

articles.title: Space Stocks Slide: SpaceX’s Starlink Push Adds To Pressure, RKLB Leads Losses, RDW Holds Up Best - Stocktwits
articles.summary: Space Stocks Slide: SpaceX’s Starlink Push Adds To Pressure, RKLB Leads Losses, RDW Holds Up Best  Stocktwits
articles.full_text:
SpaceX (SPCX) weathered this week's space-stock selloff better than AST SpaceMobile (ASTS), Rocket Lab (RKLB) and Firefly Aerospace (FLY), but Redwire (RDW) held up best as launch setbacks and competitive concerns overshadowed fresh contract wins.
SPCX fell 9% over the past week, compared with declines of 13% for ASTS, 19% for RKLB and FLY each. RDW lost 6.99%, the smallest drop among the five popular space stocks.
SpaceX entered the week with momentum behind its Starlink Mobile ambitions. An FCC order from last week authorized a 15,000-satellite direct-to-device constellation, followed by Grain Management’s agreement to sell its nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio to SpaceX. The spectrum transaction remains subject to FCC approval with a reported price of $8 billion.
However, the expansion plans faced political scrutiny this week. Ukraine said restrictions on SpaceX’s satellite service disrupted drone operations, while Musk said the U.S. government controlled military Starshield usage limits. On Thursday, Britain’s defense minister said that he and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth welcomed the restoration of Starlink service.
Meanwhile, Barclays suggested that a Tesla-SpaceX merger announcement could come before Tesla’s Dec.6 annual meeting. Another highlight was the latest flying Roadster reveal, which highlighted the companies’ engineering ties.
On Stocktwits, SPCX retail sentiment slipped to ‘bearish’ from ‘bullish’ levels a week ago amid ‘normal’ message volume. Shares are down 8% year-to-date.
Rocket Lab took the biggest hit after announcing this week that Neutron’s first flight is now expected in 2027, beyond its previous fourth-quarter 2026 target. The update identified air pockets in a carbon-composite dome for the first-stage propellant tank. Rocket Lab said it changed the manufacturing process and was building a replacement, with assembly and testing still needed before setting a firmer launch date.
Neutron is key to the company’s push into larger launch missions. Shares fell 7% to $55.25 on Thursday, extending their losing streak to seven sessions. ARK leaned into the weakness, buying 168,633 shares across three ETFs, worth about $9.32 million at Thursday’s close. Rocket Lab also highlighted its hardware’s role in NASA’s Perseverance mission after the rover set a distance record on Oct.11.
On Stocktwits, RKLB retail sentiment improved to ‘bullish’ from ‘neutral’ levels a week ago amid ‘high’ message volume. Shares are down 21% year-to-date.
AST SpaceMobile faced opposing analyst calls as investors weighed its carrier partnerships against SpaceX’s expanding mobile ambitions. Deutsche Bank upgraded ASTS to ‘Buy’ from ‘Hold’ on Monday, maintaining a $93 target and calling the selloff a buying opportunity.
On the other hand, Piper Sandler cut the stock to ‘Neutral’ from ‘Overweight’ and lowered its target to $54 from $98, citing launch-schedule uncertainty and competitive risks. Clear Street kept ‘Buy’ and a $115 target, saying that ASTS was six months ahead in direct-to-cell service and that both companies face launch risks. BlueBirds 14, 15 and 16 had already reached Cape Canaveral, but investors were still waiting for a firm launch date.
On Stocktwits, ASTS retail sentiment slipped to ‘bullish’ from ‘extremely bullish’ levels a week ago amid ‘high’ message volume. Shares are down 39% year-to-date.
Redwire paired the group’s smallest decline with a busy week of operational announcements. On Monday, the company said that the final pair of its Roll-Out Solar Array wings would launch to the International Space Station aboard NASA’s SpaceX CRS-35 cargo mission. Six wings are already deployed, with the full eight-wing system expected to provide more than 160 kilowatts of power.
The company then announced about $13.8 million in additional Stalker drone orders for the National Guard on Thursday, supporting training for the Army’s new Tactical UAS Specialist role. It also introduced the Octopus 140 infrared imaging payload on Tuesday.
However, Piper Sandler initiated coverage at ‘Neutral’ with an $11 target. The brokerage wants more evidence that Redwire’s products can compete successfully across space and defense markets.
On Stocktwits, RDW retail sentiment slipped to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ levels a week ago amid ‘normal’ message volume. Shares are up 17% year-to-date.
Firefly had fewer fresh announcements. On Wednesday, it scheduled third-quarter results for Nov.10 after the market closes. The update followed unit SciTec’s announcement from last week of a $1.5 million U.S. Air Force contract extension, taking the total to $31 million. The work adds counter-drone sensor feeds to a battle-management system.
Firefly also entered the debate over AST SpaceMobile’s acquisition options. Satellite consultant Tim Farrar suggested that AST could consider “a launch company (e.g. Firefly)” for a smaller deal, while warning that its opportunity to follow Rocket Lab’s acquisition playbook could be narrowing.
On Stocktwits, RDW retail sentiment slipped to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ levels a week ago amid ‘high’ message volume. Shares are down % year-to-date.

articles.title: Starlink Speed Limits Cripple Ukraine's Drone, Air Defense - 조선일보
articles.summary: Starlink Speed Limits Cripple Ukraine's Drone, Air Defense  조선일보
articles.full_text:
Ukraine’s military, which has relied on drones as a core force on both offensive and defensive fronts for over four years since Russia’s invasion, has faced a critical setback. This is because the operation of StarShield, a military version of the U.S.-based commercial satellite internet service Starlink, was abruptly restricted on the 14th, causing drones to become uncontrollable and disrupting operations.
Starlink, operated by Elon Musk’s space company SpaceX, provides services to remote areas where conventional high-speed internet is unavailable through a dense network of low-Earth orbit satellites. SpaceX began testing satellite launches for Starlink in 2018 and, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 destroyed existing communication networks, Musk supplied Ukraine with approximately 20,000 antenna and terminal sets.
However, Reuters and BBC reported that the StarShield service, which Ukrainian forces used to connect drones, was restricted without prior notice. Some critics argue this highlights Ukraine’s limitations in relying on the goodwill of specific countries and corporations. Serhiy Beskrestnov, a military advisor to the Ukrainian presidential office, confirmed, “We verified that SpaceX has limited the operating speed of moving Starlink terminals to 160 km/h.” A source from the 7th Rapid Response Corps, deployed in southeastern Ukraine, told Reuters, “Even at speeds of 110–120 km/h, connections were disrupted for 10–20 seconds, making drone control difficult. We had to cancel some missions.” Typically, terminals provided to Ukraine operate without issues at speeds of 400–700 km/h. The operational speed has now dropped to one-sixth of the usual level.
As the speed restrictions on StarShield disrupted drone operations, anger and frustration spread across Ukraine. Speculation dominates that this could be retaliation after Ukraine protested President Donald Trump’s lifting of sanctions on Russian oil. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in a TV interview ahead of a meeting with U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London, said, “I personally feel betrayed by Trump.” Regarding the incident, Musk wrote on X, “The StarShield system is owned and controlled by the U.S. government, and all restrictions on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. president.” He added, “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX and cannot be used for offensive military actions.” While Musk claims the two systems are separate, analysts suggest the U.S. government is behind the restrictions, as both systems share the same satellite-based technology.
Ukraine’s military uses StarShield terminals on drones for long-range attacks and to intercept Russian drone strikes. Instead of ground-based stations destroyed by Russian airstrikes, they rely on a network built from 7,000–8,000 low-Earth orbit satellites operating at altitudes of around 500 km. This minimizes interference on the battlefield. Additionally, first-person view (FPV) kamikaze drones can transmit real-time video until impact, maximizing mission success.
However, with speed limits now below typical racing drones (around 200 km/h), Ukraine’s drone capabilities—once praised as the world’s strongest—have crumbled. The issue extends beyond offensive operations: gaps have emerged in air defense. Russia deployed the Geran-4, a jet-engine-modified version of the Iranian Shahed-136 drone, in summer 2024, attacking central Kyiv. Ukraine’s failure to intercept these drones led to civilian casualties. The Geran-4’s top speed is reportedly 500 km/h.
A Ukrainian military source lamented, “At the current service speed, interception is difficult.” The Guardian noted, “After Russia deployed jet-powered drones, Ukraine’s interception rate dropped from 90% to 60%,” and warned it could fall further if restrictions continue. Since Ukraine also uses drones for frontline supply missions, operational disruptions are expected to persist.
This incident has exposed the vulnerability of a war swayed by specific corporations and leaders. Trump, on the 10th, criticized Zelenskyy over protests against lifting sanctions on Russian oil, saying, “Ukraine needs a new leader.” Musk echoed this the next day, writing, “It’s time for Ukraine to find a new leader.” Analysts argue this situation shows how Ukraine’s drone capabilities could be swayed by Trump and Musk’s interests and moods.
Meanwhile, Russia continued its assault on the 14th, launching 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 attack drones targeting Kyiv, Kharkiv, and other cities. The New York Times described this as the largest single ballistic missile attack since the war began.

articles.title: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
articles.summary: Research suggests listening more while talking less. Killing aimless meetings can help, too.
articles.full_text:
Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives.
Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior.
Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect, communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior.Read full article

articles.title: Daily briefing: Bleached corals revived by healthy neighbour’s touch
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 15 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03336-0Ghostly white corals are fully restored in eight weeks by contact with a healthy counterpart. Plus, arXiv is capping submissions per researcher and four good news stories to brighten your day.
articles.full_text:
Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.
Bleached coral revived by healthy touch
Scientists have successfully restored bleached coral in the lab by placing it in contact with a healthy fragment. Researchers found that when a healthy piece of Pocillopora damicornis coral rested against a bleached piece, the two fused together to create a bridge across which algal symbionts can spread. This transfer fully restored the bleached coral within eight weeks, even if the healthy piece was removed after a week. The result “can inspire solutions that eventually may be scalable” to reverse widespread coral decline, says marine ecologist and study co-author Fiorenza Micheli.
Reference: Science Advances paper
arXiv tries to close AI floodgates
The preprint server arXiv has introduced a cap of two papers per month for each submitting researcher in a bid to clampdown on a deluge of submissions, many generated by artificial intelligence. The limit is the latest measure to prevent its voluntary moderators from being overwhelmed by submissions, says astrophysicist Steinn Sigurðsson, scientific director of arXiv. Some researchers support the cap; others counter that it doesn’t solve the root problem. AI slop will “simply go somewhere else and become someone else’s problem”, says Natalie Khalil, the founder of AI-assisted peer-review platform Reviewer3.
Brown fat comes with big benefits
A study of more than 100,000 people has revealed some surprising benefits of brown fat — a type that burns calories to generate heat. Researchers found that people with ‘active’ brown fat are less affected by health issues — such as type 2 diabetes, depression and anxiety — than those without it. The risk of these conditions decreased the more active brown fat a person had. The study is retrospective, so can’t confirm that brown fat is causing these benefits, but “it’s still a very interesting and surprising study”, says molecular biologist Irfan Lodhi.
Bouba–Kiki effect holds true in dogs
When presented with two shapes, one with spikes and one rounded, and asked to designate them ‘bouba’ and ‘kiki’, people tend to agree that kiki is the spiky one — and so do dogs. Researchers found that when presented with images of these shapes, domestic dogs (Canis familiaris) more often looked at and moved toward the round shape when the word ‘bouba’ was played from a speaker, and vice versa. The results could suggest that dogs make similar connections between visual information and sounds to humans.
Reference: Proceedings of the Royal Society B paper
Features & opinion
Four science stories to brighten your day
Nature’s latest collection of stories selected to bring readers joy includes the newest penguin species described by science, and news that the island nation of Mauritius has become the first country in the world to reduce its number of people with type 2 diabetes — an impressive feat with diabetes rates rising globally, researchers say.
Many microorganisms; one test
A technique called metagenomic testing can screen for every microorganism that might be present in a sample, rather than searching for one in particular. Now hospitals are trialling ways of using these tests to quickly identify whether acute illnesses that cause neurological symptoms are bacterial, viral or autoimmune in origin to inform more effective treatment. Interpreting the results of metagenomic tests — which pick up pathogens, harmless microbes and contamination alike — can be a rate-limiting step, but advances in AI have enabled a faster sort of useful data from noise.
How to be an American scientist
The US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine has updated On Being a Scientist, its bible for graduate students and early career researchers first published in 1989. Things have changed since the last edition, in 2009, note engineer Mitul Luhar, chemist and dean Emily Pentzer and psychologist Alan Leshner, who was formerly head of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. “Shifts in research priorities and funding place new expectations and pressures on scientists,” they write. “Early-career researchers feel the consequences most acutely.”
