Amid wars, AI doom and a super El Niño, good news can seem in short supply. But it is there if you go looking. In Nature’s latest collection of stories selected to bring readers joy, learn about a country that has reversed its rates of diabetes and umbrella that keep corals cool.
But first, you might have heard about reports of the first new wild cat species in a century, announced last month1. The spotted feline, called Leopardus tilcayo, was found in the forested Yungas region of Bolivia.
But did you know that a new member has also been inducted into the penguin family this year? A population of penguins on the remote Kerguelen Islands — around 2,000 kilometres north of Antarctica in the Indian Ocean — has been designated as a new species, the southeastern gentoo (Pygoscelis kerguelensis)2. This addresses a long-running debate about whether the gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua) is one species or several. Using genetic analysis, scientists say the southeastern gentoo is its own species and that three populations previously identified as subspecies of gentoo should also be considered their own species.
Meanwhile, two new species of sea spider3 have been found in the Salish Sea, off the west coast of the United States and Canada. Sea spiders are a type of marine arthropod related to horseshoe crabs and arachnids. One of the new species, Callipallene pilosuspedes, has four bright red eyes, legs three times as long as its body, a triangular mouth and a short proboscis with claws it uses to grab food. It also uses spiny appendages at the bottom of its head, called ovigers, to groom itself. The other species, called Tanystylum kiixin, has stubby legs, an hourglass-shaped body and black eyes.
Diabetes rates go down
Mauritius has become the first country in the world to reduce its number of people with type 2 diabetes4. Researchers say this is impressive, given that rates of the disease are rising globally.
The island nation off the east coast of Africa has been surveying how many people have type 2 diabetes or raised blood sugar levels — an indicator of being at risk of developing diabetes — since 1987. The number of people with the condition went up between 1987 and 2009, but had decreased by 11% for men and 16% for women by 2021. Rates of raised blood sugar also decreased by roughly one-third between 2009 and 2021.
The trend is striking, write Shukri Mohamed and Andre Pascal, at the African Population and Health Research Center in Nairobi, in a commentary5 accompanying the study in The Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology. It is probably the result of improved awareness of diabetes, they say, as well as better screening and access to health care.
Umbrellas for coral
Improvised umbrellas made from cloth resistant to ultraviolet light protected a small section of coral reef in the Florida Keys from heat stress during extreme temperatures in 20246. Scientists made umbrella-like canopies using PVC pipes, filled with spray foam, and shade cloth; the structures floated about 30 centimetres above the coral.
This shading reduced the amount of solar radiation the coral was exposed to, minimizing the heat stress that often causes coral bleaching by killing tiny, coloured organisms that live inside the coral. Nearby unshaded corals, by comparison, continued to get paler over time. The research team says that similar shades could be a cheap, effective way to protect coral against heat stress.

Maia Weinstock is deputy editorial director at MIT News, a lecturer on the history of women in STEM at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, and an author.
Margaret Hamilton — a titan of computer science — has died aged 90. She is best known for her work in developing the software for NASA’s Apollo project, which landed the first humans on the Moon.
Hamilton’s influence on the field of computing was vast. A specialist in systems engineering and human–computer interaction, she helped to develop pioneering techniques for reliable computer programming and is often credited with coining the term ‘software engineering’. Her work on logical procedures and systems that worked even in the presence of errors helped to give software development comparable stature to the development of computer hardware.
In addition to her work on Apollo at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, Hamilton ventured out on her own as a software entrepreneur, founding companies that specialized in programming languages and systems used in numerous fields, from space and defence to energy, communications and more.
Hamilton was born Margaret Heafield in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936. Her parents later moved the family to Michigan and encouraged her to explore her considerable talents in both technical and humanities subjects. She began undergraduate studies at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor before transferring to Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, where she completed a bachelor of arts in mathematics with a minor in philosophy in 1958.
The next year, Hamilton moved with her first husband, James Cox Hamilton, to Boston, Massachusetts. The two had met at Earlham — he a chemist and the student-body president; she a maths whiz and the homecoming queen, according to their daughter, Lauren. Forgoing her original plan to attend graduate school, Margaret began working with Edward Lorenz, the founder of modern chaos theory — in which tiny variations in large systems can cause major unpredictable changes — in the MIT meteorology department, while James attended law school. With no previous programming experience, Hamilton helped to develop weather-prediction software using the LGP-30, a 31-bit computer with a 4,096-word memory.
In 1961, by then a working mother, Hamilton moved to a new project at the MIT Lincoln Laboratory: coding for the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE), a defence system being developed to ward off air attacks by the Soviet Union. Her stellar work on SAGE paid off. When she heard a few years later that a lab on MIT’s main campus was recruiting programmers to send men to the Moon, her application was swiftly advanced. She became the first programmer hired for the Apollo project at MIT, at a time when women made up just a tiny fraction of the workforce in US science and engineering. Although the vast majority of NASA’s Apollo project team was male, Hamilton was joined by a number of women who made key contributions in maths, coding, engineering and more.
Hamilton was tapped to head the team tasked with writing and testing software for the Apollo Guidance Computer. The space race was in full swing, and engineers and programmers at the MIT Instrumentation Lab were under high pressure to achieve what had only ever been dreamt of before, both quickly and safely. Hamilton stated in subsequent years that “there was no choice but to be pioneers”.

Build your slide template
Employ colours, typography and layouts
Building a slide template starts with three foundational choices — colours, fonts and layouts. This article covers the basics of colour theory and how to build a reusable palette, the essentials of typography, including serif, sans-serif, handwritten and monospace fonts, plus the finer points of kerning and leading, and why a near-blank layout might serve you better than the prescribed layouts that ship with your slideware.
14 October 2026
This article is part of a series:
Most knowledge workers who want to make presentations don’t think of themselves as designers. It’s fair to say the visual design of presentations is daunting enough to consume most presenters' mental space. Perhaps that’s why we equate the slides with the presentation.
Visual design is a broad subject, so we can’t cover it in its entirety. However, it’s important enough that the next few articles in this series will focus on slide design. I’ll begin with some fundamentals. Imagine I had to create a presentation about the content of this article. If I had to create a title slide for that deck, I might make it look like the one below. It juxtaposes a few elements — an image, text and some colours — into a layout.
Figure 1: A simple title slide combines an image, some text and light-handed colours.
If I were to continue building these slides, I’d have to make some recurring design decisions. Instead, I embed these decisions into a template. We’ll discuss what it takes to set up your own template, but first let’s address an elephant in the room.
The corporate template
If you work at a large enough corporation, your employer may have provided a corporate slide template. There are good reasons for this. Most people aren’t adept at assembling slides, so it helps to codify some default layouts in a template. People often use colours and fonts that may clash with the brand’s aesthetic, and a template can place some guardrails to avoid these errors.
The trouble with standard templates is that everyone uses the defaults. Before you know it, everyone’s slides look the same. People ignore boring things, so there’s value in breaking that monotony.
Now, if you can understand what your marketing colleagues are trying to achieve with their prescribed templates, you can adhere to your corporate brand and assemble slides that look unique. Through the rest of this article, I’ll show you how to build your own template, but you can also use that advice to unpack the key elements of any corporate slide template.
Start with a colour palette
As a self-taught designer, I’ve often struggled with making colours play well with each other. For some people, colour choice is intuitive. When you reuse the same colours in all slides of your presentation, the visuals gain a cohesive identity.
It’s helpful to understand the basics of colour theory, so you know which colour palette might work for your presentation style. The colour wheel is a good starting point. Think of it as an abstract illustration of the colour spectrum that helps you understand which colours work well together.
Figure 2: A basic colour wheel.
When you examine the wheel, you’ll notice that the closer the colours are to the centre, the less intense they are. Colours at the periphery are more saturated. There lies lesson one. If your slide background will be white or light, choose colours that sit at the periphery. If you want your slide background dark, choose colours that sit close to the centre.
Figure 3: Colours at the periphery work well with light slides. Those towards the centre work well with darker backgrounds.
There are many ways to choose colours and build your palette.
| Approach | What it is | Colour wheel | 
|---|---|---|
| Complementary colours | These colours sit on opposite ends of the wheel. Placing them together creates a strong, high-contrast colour scheme. |  | 
| Analogous colours | These colours sit close to each other on the wheel. When you use them together, you’ll end up with a minimalist, elegant colour scheme. |  | 
| Evenly-spaced colours | If you choose colours evenly spaced across the colour wheel, you’ll end up with a colourful scheme with reasonable contrast between them. This approach is a variation of the complementary colours approach. |  | 
| Triads | By choosing shades that form a triangle on the colour wheel, you get a tight variation on the evenly spaced colour scheme approach. |  | 
| Tetrads | You can extend the concept of triads by drawing a square on the colour wheel and adding another colour to your scheme. |  | 
| Monochromatic | If you want a super-minimalist approach, choose different shades of the same colour by drawing a straight line on the colour wheel. |  | 
Adobe provides you with a free, interactive colour palette generator to play around with the colour wheel and land on a theme you like. You can build your palette from scratch, browse trending palettes, and even generate them from a photograph that represents the content you want to present.
Figure 4: Generating a colour palette from a representative image.
The advantage of working with palettes is that software like PowerPoint lets you swap themes across your entire presentation without updating every diagram. Choose a new theme, and PowerPoint recolours all your diagrams and slides. The interactive demo below shows you how you can swap your colour palettes in PowerPoint.
But here’s a word of caution. Resist the temptation to invent a new colour palette for every presentation. As a corporate presenter, I’ve found it helpful to find or create a palette that I like and then stick with it for months, often years.
If you work for a large corporation, someone else has likely already defined a colour palette. For example, at Thoughtworks, our corporate palette has six colours, plus black and a light grey shade. Since most of these colours are dark, I use them on a light background.
Figure 5: The Thoughtworks colour palette.
Over the years, I’ve built a diagram library that reuses the same colour palette, so if a presentation references one of my core ideas, I incorporate a representative diagram into a Thoughtworks slide deck. It’s the compounding benefit of using the same, boring colour palette.
Figure 6: A reusable diagram library for my book that leverages the Thoughtworks palette.
Novice designers often use too many colours in the quest to build colourful slides. Now that you know a bit about colour theory, you’ll realise that if you pick too many colours from the wheel, you’ll struggle to establish a theme and a visual identity that’s evident across your slides. So, choose a restricted colour palette instead. Limit yourself to six colours, then add black and white to the palette. Less is more. As a bonus, consider all shades of grey as free additions.
Next, pick the fonts you’ll use
As presenters, we needn’t be experts in the dark art of typography. Most presentations need only two or three fonts. Sometimes, one font face is plenty. Consistency beats variety.
But here are the basics. There are two types of fonts, each with its own merits — serif and sans-serif. Serif fonts have little feet, i.e. the serifs. Sans-serif fonts literally lack serifs. The image below shows the difference.
Figure 7: Serif fonts have little feet and extensions. Sans-serif fonts don’t have them.
If you’re reading this article on martinfowler.com, you’ll notice the website’s serif typeface. And that’s a great use of serif fonts. They’re more suited to reading and paragraph text. This is also why newspapers still use serif fonts.
Sans-serif fonts, on the other hand, suit billboards and signage better. When you drive around your town, look at the fonts on large advertisements. It’s likely they employ sans-serif fonts. Presentation slides are more like billboards than magazine pages.
So, if you had to default to one kind of typeface for your presentations, I’d recommend picking a sans-serif font. They work well for online presentations, where the resolution is often a maximum of 1080p or 720p, and just as well for keynotes in large auditoriums with state-of-the-art projectors.
However, there’s no harm in mixing and matching fonts. You could use a serif font for titles and a sans-serif font for the rest of the text. The key is to stay consistent and avoid what Neal Ford calls the “fontaholic” antipattern.
A Fontaholic is someone who believes using a cacophony of fonts will “jazz up” a presentation. Disharmonic fonts are jarring. They make presentations gruesome and more difficult to read.
Here’s an example of a slide that uses a serif font for the title and a sans-serif font for everything else.
Figure 8: Mixing and matching serif and sans-serif fonts.
Limiting the number of fonts in your presentation shouldn’t limit your creativity. Modern, variable-weight fonts allow you many variations for the same typeface.
Figure 9: Variable-weight fonts offer you a lot of versatility.
Aside from serif and sans-serif fonts, I’ll advocate for two more font types.
Handwritten fonts
I suggest using these fonts only for annotations. They’re excellent at breaking the pattern and monotony of your standard fonts, and that’s handy when you want to draw your audience’s attention to a specific part of your presentation. For example, in the slide below, the red, handwritten font appears after each part of the diagram builds, drawing the audience’s attention to the compounding benefits of the AI flywheel.
Figure 10: You can use a handwritten font for annotations and break the visual monotony.
Monospace fonts
If you’re a developer and you often show code snippets in presentations, I suggest adding a monospace font to your repertoire. In code, spacing is part of the meaning. A monospace font gives every character equal width and helps you maintain indentation, columns, and structure. Your code is easier to scan and far easier to explain on a slide. Abstract
Spirocyclic frameworks, polycyclic structures in which two rings share a single carbon atom, constitute key structural motifs across diverse areas, including optoelectronic and hole-transporting materials1–3, ligand design for coordination complexes4–6, and numerous natural products7. In a spiro skeleton, the two molecular units adopt an orthogonal arrangement, generating a rigid three-dimensional (3D) architecture. Introducing a single carbon atom to join two components to form the spiro centre therefore represents a direct strategy for constructing such frameworks. Previous carbon-atom-transfer approaches have largely relied on π-bond reactivity, whereas controlled insertion of a carbon atom into C–C σ-bonds remains challenging8–11. Here we report a rhodium-catalysed spiro-carbon-atom insertion reaction that converts biphenylene substrates into spirocyclic structures through sequential C–C bond activation. Using N-isocyanoiminophosphorane (PINC)12–14 as an atomic carbon equivalent, the reaction forms four new C–C bonds at a spiro centre. The transformation enables both homo- and cross-spirofusion of biphenylenes and can be extended to reactions combining σ- and π-bond activation. These results establish a catalytic strategy for constructing structurally complex spirocyclic frameworks through C–C σ-bond activation, with a single carbon atom serving as a central linchpin.

articles.title: Becoming real
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03114-yAn endless blessing.
articles.full_text:
After they had enclosed the humans, they did not make the wall very high.
“Why not build it higher?” the child asked.
“High walls are for those who want to escape,” the old man said. “We don’t.”
The child sat on the threshold and stared at the pale line in the distance. Beyond the wall, the light never went out. It looked like another sky, one that had forgotten how to sleep.
“What is out there?” he asked.
“No people coughing through winter. No clocks losing time. No old men who forget names,” the old man said. “And no peaches that will rot by tomorrow.”
The child thought about that. “That sounds good.”
The old man did not answer. He broke the peach in his hands. Juice ran through his fingers, and the air filled at once with sweetness. At the edges, the flesh had already begun to brown, as though dusk had touched it.
“Eat. It won’t be good much longer.”
“Why do things smell better when they’re about to go bad?”
“Because you know they won’t stay.”
Read more science fiction from Nature Futures
That was when the figure appeared. It came monthly to the village entrance. It had the shape and voice of a person, but was simply too complete — symmetrical, unmarred and terrifyingly still.
“That is decaying,” it said.
“So?” The child hid it behind his back.
“So it is imperfect.”
The child made a face. “You always get those two words mixed up.”
The figure fell quiet, then turned to the old man. “The knife-grinder died yesterday. I saw him three days ago, sharpening an old blade. If he knew he was ending, why bother with a tool he would never use again?”
“Did you come to ask about the grinder, or yourself?” the old man asked.
A brittle leaf drifted onto the figure’s shoulder. It lifted it, studying it like a rare manuscript. “We can manufacture this. The fractals, the insect marks. But we cannot create this specific instance of loss.”
“Because it was not made; it was lived,” the old man said. “What you are looking at is time. Not the time of your servers, but the kind that settles onto things and makes them worn and unique. In your world, nothing is ever ‘now’ because everything is forever.”
“There is a sickness where I come from,” the figure said. “More of us are refusing back-ups. Some deliberately preserve cracks in their chassis. They are seeking something called The Single-Life Accord.”
“To become nonrepeatable?” the old man asked.
“Yes. Like dying.”
Silence fell. A distant cough, the creak of a laundry line. Sounds of a world constantly wearing itself out.
“We thought preservation was victory,” the figure said. “But what is preserved does not come closer to being alive. It becomes only an exhibit. We have no fate.”
“Fate means reaching for a thing knowing it will end,” the old man said. “Living this hour carefully because it can never be retrieved from a cloud server. You have infinity. But without a frame, a painting is just an endless smear of colour.”
The child tossed his peach pit. “Without school, vacation wouldn’t be fun.”
The figure looked at the child. “But death brings terror. It brings the cessation of the ‘I’.”
“Of course,” the old man said. “That fear is the price of the ticket. Without the risk of losing yourself, you never truly possessed yourself.”
The light beyond the wall flared sharply. The figure straightened. “The Accord has been ratified. The system will allow the transition for those who confirm.”
“Will you do it?” the child asked.
“Yes.”
“Aren’t you scared?”
“I am terrified,” the figure said. “Which is how I know I am moving in the right direction.”

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02442-3A researcher in Latin America seeks advice on the best way to present themselves when applying for faculty positions in Europe and North America.

After more than 20 years of academic research, supervision and contributions to engineering technology in Latin America, I’ve been pursuing faculty positions at universities in North America and Europe. The advertised positions match my expertise closely, but my applications have been consistently unsuccessful.
The reason only became clear through a candid exchange with a colleague who had served on a selection committee for one such position. My scientific qualifications, he noted, were competitive. The factor that stopped the committee choosing me was that I hadn’t obtained grant funding from the national research system of the country I wanted to move to.
This is a problem with how funding is structured in most research-intensive countries. Grant mechanisms are often national and tied to taxpayer-supported programmes that do not enable researchers based abroad to be awarded principal-investigator status. International collaboration is actively encouraged in research, but international leadership of funded projects is another matter entirely. The practical consequence is that no amount of scientific output or achievement by an individual can compensate for this gap.
Is there anything that an applicant can do to combat this bias? — An excluded international scholar
The advice
César Marín, an ecologist at Santo Tomás University in Santiago, Chile, agrees with you. “Demonstrating experience and success on getting national funds seem to be the main hiring criteria in many countries — regardless of strong publication and supervision record,” he affirms.
In general, experience of a local system “can be an implicit metric in academia”, notes Laura Ación, co-executive director of MetaDocencia, a capacity-building organization for researchers from Spanish-speaking communities. MetaDocencia’s research on the career paths of Latin American scientists1 suggests that, as Ación says, “a lack of competitiveness for European or US funding constitutes a structural disadvantage”.
This can take a toll on academic jobseekers. “I believe that, as a foreigner, I am behind the competition for many reasons,” explains Renan Lyra, a Brazilian psychology researcher who is currently searching for positions in the United Kingdom. He suspects that one of the reasons is that researchers doing UK degrees are trained to put together domestic grant applications, and are more likely to be involved in such applications with senior researchers. Experience in bringing in money is what hiring organizations really care about, Lyra thinks.
Even researchers moving between well-resourced systems notice the gap between them. Caroline Lynn Kamerlin started her independent career in Sweden before moving to the United States as a professor. She’s now a computational chemist at the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta.
During the transition, she encountered what you describe: “When US hiring committees saw my CV, the biggest thing they saw was that I had no US funding, and the fact that I had clearly been able to get funding from several sources in Europe was not something they considered.”
One reason for hiring managers’ funding bias might be that they are familiar with certain grants, which come with a kind of brand recognition that is associated with high quality. But this can be problematic if the assumption is “that global-south grant processes are not as strict as those from the global north”, Marín comments. “On my own experience of reviewing grants for European and Latin American countries, this is not always the case.”
As you identify, this is a structural problem, so there are limits to what a single person can do. Still, there are ways for individuals to increase their chances of being hired, even in an unjust system.
Grant strategies
One way of boosting your grant track record is by forming international collaborations. But as you note, collaboration doesn’t necessarily build to leadership. And in the United States, restrictions on grants involving foreign researchers are making international collaborations of all types more challenging.
Marco Seeber, a science-policy researcher at the University of Agder in Kristiansand, Norway, says you shouldn’t underestimate the importance of trust and personal connections in the systems you’re trying to break into. The first stage could be attending and presenting at conferences, and using that as a jumping-off point for collaboration.
“I cannot emphasize strongly enough how vital it is to cultivate a diverse, robust network and community throughout a scientific career,” Ación adds. This should be reciprocal, not transactional. For instance, it can include service to scientific associations. That kind of network-building could eventually pave the way for entry into another country’s research system.
Even if you aren’t successful in getting a grant on which you’re a principal investigator (PI) in the desired country, that might not be a deal-breaker. “I think being a PI on international grants is always helpful, but it’s not absolutely necessary, just because there are so few international grants and those that exist are incredibly competitive,” Kamerlin says. If it’s still important to you to be a PI, it’s possible that the other collaborators in your consortium would be happy to have that administrative burden taken off their hands, and for you to take on the leadership role.
Some funding calls are geared towards foreign researchers of different levels, which could help you to develop a track record in the research system you’re interested in. Kamerlin highlights the European Research Council (ERC) funding schemes. “The ERC specifically wants to attract and retain the best talent in Europe, and actively encourages non-Europeans to apply to move to Europe,” she says. Admittedly, success rates are low. ERC starting grants, which are geared towards early-career researchers and can come with extra funding for researchers moving to the European Union, had a success rate of about 12% in 2025.
More broadly, in 2025, the European Commission kicked off the Choose Europe initiative to attract researchers to the EU. Although one impetus was to draw in researchers from the United States who are disillusioned with the cuts to science funding there, in principle, applicants can be of any nationality.

articles.title: Nature Index reveals the four countries to watch in biomedical engineering
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03204-xThese nations are making their distinct mark in the field through specialization and collaboration.
articles.full_text:
Biomedical-engineering research output has grown rapidly in the Nature Index. Between 2021 and 2025, the number of papers related to the field increased by 70%, a higher rate of increase than the growth of the database as a whole. This is also reflected by the subject’s proportion of all articles in the database, which rose from 2.4% to 2.7%. Within this expansion, however, the field’s research landscape has also shifted, with countries’ relative contributions reflecting changing patterns of international collaboration and research specialization.
The clearest trend is that between 2021 and 2025, biomedical-engineering research — in keeping with many other disciplines — moved decisively towards the leading nation, China. The country’s contribution to global output rose from 28.9% to 50.9%, while the field went from representing 2.8% of its total Nature Index output in 2021 to 3.5% in 2025.
The United States and Germany retained second and third place, respectively, throughout the period, but their focus on the field remained relatively static at around 2.3% to 2.5% of all output.
Here, we focus on four other countries among the leading ten in 2025 whose performance in biomedical engineering reveals more nuanced trends.
South Korea seems to have held a top-five position by developing and maintaining a strong specialization in the subject; Switzerland stands out for drawing on private-sector research and international collaboration to remain a leading European centre; Canada is one of the field’s fastest-rising countries; and the Netherlands has recorded more modest growth but retains a highly international network.
South Korea
Leading university in biomedical engineering, 2021–25: Yonsei University
Most cited paper, 2021–25: ‘Superstrong, superstiff, and conductive alginate hydrogels’ (2022)1
South Korea is an outlier among the leading nations in biomedical engineering in the Nature Index. Its research is unusually concentrated in the field, with 4.8% of its overall database output from 2021 to 2025 being in the subject, the highest percentage among the leading 25 countries. South Korea is also relatively less reliant on international collaboration compared with the three other countries featured in this article, with a little over half its papers in 2021–25 co-authored by researchers outside the country.
Nature Index 2026 Biomedical engineering
This clear specialization in biomedical engineering has helped South Korea to cement itself as one of the top-five contributors to the field, consistently ranking fourth in Share, a position that is three places higher than its overall ranking in the Nature Index. It was also the third-fastest growing nation by increase in Share in biomedical engineering between 2021 and 2025.
The country’s most cited paper in the field over the period, produced by a group from Sungkyunkwan University in Seoul and published in Nature Communications1 in 2022, explains the development of an exceptionally strong and electrically conductive seaweed-derived hydrogel. Although the paper gained almost 450 citations up to July 2026, it was not as highly cited as the top papers from the three other countries featured here. There might be multiple reasons for this, but one possible factor might be that the paper was authored solely by researchers from one institution, whereas the other research articles featured authors based in a mix of different institutions and locations.
Canada
Leading university in biomedical engineering, 2021–25: University of Toronto
Most cited paper, 2021–25: ‘A proximity-dependent biotinylation map of a human cell’ (2021)2
Canada’s Share in biomedical engineering rose by almost 60% between 2021 and 2025, making it the country with the second-largest growth in output over the period among the leading ten nations, after China. Most of Canada’s growth occurred between 2021 and 2022, when its Share rose by 51% in one year alone. Part of this rise might have been due to the addition of health-sciences journals to the database in 2022. However, these new journals grew the Nature Index overall by 13%, suggesting that Canada still excelled that year in biomedical engineering.
Unlike South Korea, however, Canada’s growth is unlikely to be related to heavy specialization: biomedical engineering was a relatively small focus of Canada’s entire output in the Nature Index, at about 2.3% of overall Share from 2021 to 2025.
Canada’s broader growth coincides with a major funding push in the life sciences that was designed to address a decline in the country’s research and biomanufacturing capacity. The decline was identified by the federal government as a reason why it was unable to produce its own COVID-19 vaccine. The government’s 2021 budget allocated Can$2.2 billion (US$1.6 billion) to a Biomanufacturing and Life Science Strategy, with money going to a mix of life-sciences and biomanufacturing companies, research institutes and universities over seven years.
Canada’s most-cited biomedical-engineering paper2 in the Nature Index from 2021 to 2025 was produced by researchers based at the Lunenfeld-Tanenbaum Research Institute in Ontario, the University of Toronto and McGill University, in Montreal. Published in Nature in 2021, the researchers showed how they constructed a detailed map of a human cell by placing molecular labels throughout the cell.
Switzerland
Leading university in biomedical engineering, 2021–25: Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich
Most cited paper, 2021–25: ‘Tissue geometry drives deterministic organoid patterning’ (2022)3
Switzerland’s biomedical-engineering Share rose from 41.5 to 49.2 between 2021 and 2025, a gain of 19%. Although its growth was modest, contributions from private-sector research have arguably helped Switzerland to maintain a spot in the top 10 each year.
From 2021 to 2025, corporate organizations were responsible for 7.2% of the country’s biomedical engineering output in the Nature Index, the highest proportion among the leading ten nations. This fits a wider pattern: Switzerland’s gross domestic expenditure on R&D stood at 3.2% of GDP in 2023, with business sector R&D alone accounting for 2.2%, well above the EU average of 1.5% — although still below South Korea’s 3.9% — according to Eurostat.

articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03247-0A tool called IdeaLens helps to judge whether concepts — rather than just writing — in scientific papers are AI-generated.

Researchers have developed a detector that aims to tell the difference between ideas made by humans and those conjured by artificial intelligence.
Used with care, IdeaLens could help to gauge the extent of AI use in submissions to conferences and journals, which have become “overwhelmed” with artificially generated content, says Rishanth Rajendhran, a computer scientist at the University of Maryland in College Park and co-author of the preprint1 describing IdeaLens.
Using AI to write scientific papers is becoming increasingly acceptable, but only “as long as the core idea” is the researcher’s own, he says.
The detector works by analysing the ‘outline’ of a work rather than the text itself. First, it distils a text — for example, a scientific paper — into an outline, stripping it of style. Then it looks for patterns that are characteristic of either AI- or human-generated ideas, such as those in arguments and flow.
The detector was able to spot AI-derived ideas 91% of the time. It “surprised me that they can detect AI-written arguments” from just the outlines, says Nikhil Garg, a computer scientist at Cornell Tech in New York City, who calls the detector impressive.
Garg cautions that because the tool is fallible, it should not be used to judge the human authenticity of individual cases, and that the detector might become inaccurate when used on types of data that are different from those used in training. “An AI ‘tell’ in one domain may simply be good human writing in another,” he says.
Structural differences
The group’s earlier work2 found that human-written stories differ structurally from those written by AI and that different chatbots tend to use the same arguments when writing essays. Together this suggested that it might be possible to make a detector for AI ideas, says Rajendhran.

articles.title: China’s AI research is booming: what it’s like to be on the front line
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03223-8China trains more AI talent than any other country. Nature spoke to analysts and scientists about how AI research there compares to the United States.
articles.full_text:

As his graduation from a top Chinese university approached earlier this year, computer scientist Lu Yi faced a tough choice. Should he move to the United States to pursue a PhD in artificial intelligence, as Chinese high-fliers have so often done before? Or should he stay in China?
The United States pays AI scientists higher salaries, has the best hardware and hosts the world’s most advanced AI laboratories. But “the gap is getting closer and closer”, says Lu, whose name has been changed because he was concerned about speaking publicly on what he saw as a sensitive issue.
AI research in China is advancing rapidly. Many more AI researchers emerge from Chinese universities than from US institutions, and graduates are increasingly opting to stay put, or to return to China after spending time in the United States. China-based researchers dominate global AI-related publications, and firms such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI make AI models with capabilities not far off those of their US rivals — and at a fraction of the price.
At the same time, the United States has become a less appealing destination for foreign researchers, with an increasingly restrictive visa system; Lu has seen friends’ applications rejected or delayed. “It’s a worry,” he says. Ultimately, Lu decided to stay in China.
The AI ecosystem in China differs in several ways from that of California’s Silicon Valley. In China, the line between academia and industry is more porous, and access to computing resources is much lower. This presents both opportunities and challenges. Chinese firms have been accused of copying US advances in their race to catch up, but they also have found techniques that make models more efficient.
“There are some that definitely think that the US is still the best place in the world to build a life and do this research, but more are questioning it,” says Scott Singer, co-director of the China AI Initiative at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Washington DC.
Where AI talent grows — and goes
China trains more AI talent than any other country. It has a pool of 51,000 active AI researchers compared with 14,000 in the United States, according to data from Digital Science (a firm operated by the Holtzbrinck Publishing Group, which has a share in Nature’s publisher, Springer Nature). The data, which are updated from a study the firm released last year1, also show that many of the researchers are at an early stage in their careers, with fewer older superstars than in the United States (see ‘Active AI researchers’).
As a proxy for studying elite researchers, many analysts have examined the origins and locations of authors at the prestigious NeurIPS conference. A study released in September by Carnegie China, a Singapore-based research centre under the umbrella of the Carnegie Endowment, reported that, on the basis of a large sample, 57% of authors at the 2025 conference had obtained their undergraduate degrees in China — up from 46% three years earlier — but that the United States was still a magnet for those studying at graduate level, pulling away around one-fifth of those undergraduates (see go.nature.com/4yfsl4v). The attraction of the United States seems to be weakening, however; Chinese scientists are increasingly staying at home, the study found. Of those researchers publishing at NeurIPS who had received undergraduate degrees in China, 69% were still there, up from 57% in 2022 (see ‘AI talent career paths’). This ability to keep top home-grown AI talent is higher than Europe’s (60%), but trails that of the United States (89%).
A related statistic is that although across all levels 63,000 Chinese students studied mathematics or computer science in the United States in 2024–25, this was 20% fewer than five years previously. One reason for this drop is that the effects of the US–China geopolitical rivalry are trickling down to research, says Grace Shao, an independent analyst covering AI and technology, based in Hong Kong. A lot of Chinese people now “feel less comfortable or a feeling of animosity amongst peers”, in the United States, she says. Every Chinese student who spoke to Nature cited visa troubles as a primary concern of going to the United States. Increasingly, visas are delayed, and the US administration has sought to limit their duration, although this is being challenged in court. Because new visa rules could affect re-entry to the United States for even existing students, some US-based Chinese nationals are too anxious to visit their home country.
Direction of travel
The data are not as clear on whether AI researchers already in the United States are flooding back to China. Media coverage tends to focus on high-profile returnees, such as Moonshot’s founder, Yang Zhilin, who created the Beijing-based company in 2023, having finished a PhD at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in 2019. But the true picture is more nuanced. A study by the Carnegie Endowment suggests that the United States is still able to retain high-profile AI researchers (see go.nature.com/3vxhdic). Of its sample of authors publishing at NeurIPS, 87% of researchers of Chinese origin — those who did their undergraduate degree in China — who had been in the United States in 2019 remained there in 2025. But the Digital Science study suggests that when looking at the changing affiliations of all AI researchers actively publishing, the net direction of flow is the US losing talent to China.
Analyses of AI-related academic papers show China ahead of the United States in terms of sheer numbers and, increasingly, influence. The Digital Science study found that China dominates academic output — by citation as well as volume — and AI-related patents. Key universities and AI firms are spread across China, with hubs in Beijing, Shanghai, Hangzhou and Shenzhen, and with 156 research organizations each publishing more than 50 AI papers a year, the study noted. Research quality is improving, too: in 2025, for the first time, the NeurIPS conference had more lead authors based in China than in the United States or Europe, according to an analysis by The Economist (see go.nature.com/4i1ka6e).
But other statistics tell a different story. Overall, the United States produces higher-impact patents and more notable AI models than China does, according to the Stanford AI Index 20262. And publication data can offer a skewed portrait of AI advances, because Chinese firms are more likely to publish scientific papers than are US start-ups, according to a preprint published in July3. Chinese academics also report high pressure to publish papers to advance their careers.
Fundamentally, the United States still makes the world’s most advanced AI. Models from OpenAI and Anthropic, both based in San Francisco, California, top the leader boards for system capabilities. “China is probably somewhere between three and seven months behind the frontier in US models,” says Singer.
One reason for the lag is that China has many fewer of the computing chips that are required to train and run cutting-edge models. Since 2022, the United States has restricted export of powerful chips known as graphics processing units (GPUs) to China, owing to national-security concerns. Chinese firms are racing to manufacture their own high-calibre chips, but none yet rivals those used by US firms.
Cash is also generally less abundant in China, with private AI investment in the United States in 2025 reaching more than 23 times that invested in China, according to the Stanford report. Chinese firms’ lack of these resources is their main bottleneck, says Shao.
Efficiency is everything
Lower access to chips and cash affects research strategies in several ways. A lack of computing resources, or ‘compute’, means, for instance, that Chinese companies are not devoting as high a volume of resources as US firms are to a process known as recursive self-improvement, says Lu. This seeks to use AI to create better models but does not guarantee success and sucks up GPU time. Shao, similarly, says that US firms have the freedom and budget to pursue more speculative research directions.
But compute constraints push researchers in China to “come up with more compute-efficient algorithms and training methods”, says Zilan Qian, who studies China’s AI development at the non-profit organization GovAI in London. For example, DeepSeek, based in Hangzhou, created its own ‘sparse attention’ mechanism, which reduces overall computation when training or using models by deciding which tokens matter most, and running calculations on the basis of those alone.
One much-debated question is to what extent Chinese companies are catching up by using a process called distillation on US models. Distillation involves either training a model on outputs from a ‘teacher’ AI, to capture a similar level of ability, or, in a more sophisticated approach that avoids direct emulation, using the teacher AI to grade and improve a smaller model’s responses. In September, the US government said that distillation campaigns formed “the core” of development by Chinese AI firms. “In the industry, the understanding is that there has definitely been distillation,” says Shao, although no one has openly acknowledged it. But in August, Zhang Yiming, founder of the Beijing-based tech firm ByteDance, which produces the Doubao chatbot, publicly rebuked the practice, telling staff to avoid distillation in favour of “long-term goals”.

articles.title: Protecting nature means valuing biodiversity
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03219-4Appeals for extra money are failing. Fundamental changes are needed to safeguard the planet for future generations.
articles.full_text:
The words of Canadian-American singer-songwriter Joni Mitchell’s 1970 environmental anthem Big Yellow Taxi will be echoing in the halls of the United Nations biodiversity conference (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia, that begins on 19 October.
Don’t it always seem to go / That you don’t know what you’ve got / Till it’s gone / They paved paradise / And put up a parking lot.
“Nature is in freefall,” according to the Living Planet Report 2026, published on 7 October by conservation charity WWF. Between 1970 and 2022, the sizes of vertebrate wildlife populations that WWF research teams have been monitoring decreased by 73% (see go.nature.com/4zy2zxd).
Lay of the land: terrestrial conservation efforts cover a wider area than thought
Almost four years ago at COP15 in Montreal, Canada, countries agreed on targets to stop and eventually reverse biodiversity loss by 2050. The goals included protecting 30% of land and water habitats by 2030 (also called the 30 × 30 target) and to substantially increase annual funding for conservation from public and private sources — to at least US$30 billion for low-income nations and small island states — by the end of the decade. Although these goals are not currently on course to be met, official figures could be underestimating the global amount of protected land, suggests a study published on 14 October (H. M. K. O’Neill et al. Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11157-4; 2026).
The Living Planet Report notes that some species are no longer considered endangered — including the Atlantic bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus) and the green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas). But if the global decline in biodiversity is to be halted, a much more fundamental change is needed: the value of natural capital and ecosystem services must be factored into nations’ decision-making.
Many of the poorest countries that are rich in biodiversity rely heavily on international public and philanthropic funding to protect their natural resources. In Montreal, countries promised to mobilize at least $200 billion per year by the end of the decade. Some estimates suggest that the world has already surpassed that: global biodiversity finance trebled from roughly $100 billion in 2019 to around $300 billion in 2024, according to reports by the Paulson Institute, a think tank in Chicago, Illinois (see go.nature.com/3vuuvfz and go.nature.com/4yhgtuc). As of June 2025, 12 national and regional governments have contributed $386 million to a biodiversity fund for low- and middle-income countries. The fund currently supports 82 projects, including initiatives backing ecotourism in Indonesia and locally managed marine conservation in Madagascar.
The problem is that spending on activities that harm nature strongly exceeds the boost to biodiversity finance. For instance, it will now cost around $1.3 trillion a year to achieve the 30 × 30 target by 2030, suggests the Paulson Institute report. Moreover, several small but important biodiversity funds are struggling. For instance, the Cali Fund, which was launched last year, has received barely any donations so far. Companies that profit from using genetic-sequence data gathered in biodiversity-rich nations are encouraged to pay into this pot. As of now, businesses have contributed a grand total of $6,000.
Biodiversity conservation has an evidence problem — it’s time to fix it
Some economists say that to save nature, the world can’t rely on public funding or voluntary contributions from businesses. Government aid to low- and middle-income countries dropped last year by 23% compared with 2024, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Researchers are instead proposing that countries cut public subsidies that harm nature and that they end or reform environment-damaging policies.
In its State of Finance for Nature 2026 report, the UN Environment Programme estimates that public spending on fossil-fuel subsidies exceeded $1 trillion in 2023 (see go.nature.com/3trvr2y). As well as harming nature, such subsidies can be counterproductive, too. Many governments, for instance, pay farmers to use pesticides that reduce the biodiversity needed for agriculture to be productive.
But cutting subsidies and even reforming them is difficult. Governments use subsidies to support businesses and protect jobs. Financial aid, including for energy and food, is also used to keep prices down for households when the cost of living is increasing.
China and many European countries are making progress by tying farm subsidies to environmental objectives, such as improved soil health, or by paying farmers to plant hedges and wildflowers. But these initiatives are in their early stages, and implementation is patchy.
Don’t rush rules for sharing digital genetic-sequence information
If aid is faltering and redirected subsidies won’t bridge the biodiversity-funding gap, something else needs to happen. Researchers argue that the people who run their nation’s economy — the ministers of finance and their teams — should be factoring the true costs of nature into their decision-making.
If, for example, a local or national government plans to convert part of a wetland for industrial use, any projections of economic benefits should be compared with the services provided by wetlands that will be lost, such as wildlife habitats, water purification and carbon sequestration. If bee populations decline because of habitat loss, their pollination services — crucial to human survival — will be lost. However, the cost of replacing such services is rarely factored in when land is converted.
For some years, China’s decision makers, together with the Natural Capital Alliance, a multidisciplinary team of researchers in China, Europe and the United States, have been studying how to incorporate such analyses into the country’s economic and industrial policies, using a concept called gross ecosystem product. Such an approach needs to be adopted by policymakers in other countries, too.
As long as countries regard ecosystems as being cost-free, they will always need appeals to altruism to protect nature — appeals that are increasingly failing. It’s encouraging that finance ministers are expected to join their environmental counterparts at COP17. Achieving the Herculean task of protecting ecosystems and biodiversity requires the world to change how it values nature.
Mitchell’s words should not become a self-fulfilling prophecy: make sure we protect nature, because “you don’t know what you’ve got till it’s gone”.

Scientists have rapidly restored bleached coral in a laboratory by placing it in contact with a healthy fragment, giving hope for reversing widespread coral decline.
Rising sea temperatures are stressing corals, causing the animals to expel the symbiotic algae that live in their tissues and give them their colour — a process known as bleaching. Because the photosynthetic algae (Symbiodiniaceae) provide corals with most of their nutrients, without them, the marine organisms are likely to starve and die.
A team of researchers has now shown that it is possible to fully reverse this bleaching process, in just days. It reported the findings in Science Advances on 14 October1.
“This incredible new result — that fast and full recovery is possible in bleached coral — can inspire solutions that eventually may be scalable,” says Fiorenza Micheli, a marine ecologist at Stanford University’s Center for Ocean Solutions in California and a co-author on the study.
The healing touch
In early 2025, marine scientist, and study co-author, Stephen Palumbi at Hopkins Marine Station in Pacific Grove, California, was working in the lab and noticed that two coral fragments in a tank were accidentally touching. Where the healthy and bleached fragment met, colour had begun to seep into the ghostly branch. “I’d never seen that before,” he remembers.
Danny Collins, who was studying how disease spreads through coral contact as part of his PhD at Stanford, set out to investigate whether algae can also spread and, if so, how.
He prepared ten pairs of coral fragments from the same animal (Pocillopora damicornis)., Each pair had a bleached and a healthy fragment. He set up five pairs so that their fragments touched each other, and five with their fragments separated by a few millimetres. In the touching pairs, the bleached coral recovered within eight weeks.
“We were blown away when we watched the colour of the algal symbionts transfer over to the bleached coral, reviving it in a very short period of time,” Collins says. By week two, the symbiont population was doubling every four days, which is much faster than the recovery times seen in studies of coral recovering naturally in the wild2,3.
After touching the healthy fragment for a week, a bleached branch could fully recover on its own, even if separated from the healthy branch.
In the slightly separated pairs, the bleached fragments died after 20 weeks.
Using high-powered microscopy, the team showed that two coral fragments fuse together by creating a tissue bridge — enabling symbiont transfer. This only occurred for coral fragments taken from an individual of the same genetic make-up, called a genet. Fragments from different species and even different animals of the same species did not fuse together, and so did not nurse the bleached piece back to health.

Biomedical engineering encompasses a broad range of research with clinical applications, from creating surgical implants to using physics to improve medical imaging. Here we focus on three researchers whose fundamental work is paving the way for such health-care solutions.
XINYU DONG: Cold comfort
Hydrogels are among a biomedical engineer’s most favoured materials, thanks to their water-rich, highly porous and elastic nature being able to closely mimic human tissue. But they face some key limitations, says Xinyu Dong: “They’re often quite fragile and their high water content makes them sensitive to dehydration and freezing when surrounding conditions change.”
Dong, a materials scientist at the National University of Singapore (NUS), creates next-generation, high-performance hydrogels using freeze casting, a technique normally used to make ceramic scaffolds that are used as 3D templates to guide bone repair. Also known as ice templating, freeze casting involves mixing a material with water to form a slurry, placing it in a mould, and then using a temperature gradient to grow ice crystals in a particular direction. This forces the slurry’s particles into the spaces between the crystals so that, after evaporating the ice, “what’s left behind is an organized network of pores” in the desired material, explains Dong.
Dong began experimenting with freeze casting in 2020 during her PhD at NUS, creating porous ceramic scaffolds that mimic the structure of bone: strong, yet able to deform to a degree without breaking1. She later applied this to aerogels — ultra-lightweight materials composed mostly of air — and hydrogels. “These materials are very different,” says Dong. “But the basic idea is the same: by controlling their structure at different scales, we can change how they behave and give them useful properties.”
In 2024, Dong proposed a twist on freeze casting2: instead of evaporating the ice after freezing, the mould is removed and soaked in a chilled organic solvent. As the ice gradually dissolves into the solvent and the organic liquid takes its place in the channels throughout the newly formed gel, the polymer walls are pulled closer together, increasing the linkages between them. The solvent also incorporates salt ions into the matrix, which makes the material electrically conductive. The result? Tougher, stronger and more stretchable skin-like organohydrogels — ideal for use in wearable electronics and soft robotics.
Dong and her collaborators described one such application this year in Nature Communications3, using an extension of this technique. “We developed a soft hydrogel-based electronic skin that formed close and stable contact with the body,” she says. When integrated into a wristband, the gel could be used to monitor skin temperature, pulse and sweat concentration.
As an undergraduate, Dong studied materials science at Soochow University in China, before switching to mechanical engineering for her PhD. This blend, she says, helps give her important insights into how a material’s properties “can be shaped through manufacturing and structural design” and “used to solve real engineering problems”.
Dong credits her father with inspiring her problem-solving skills from a young age. He often travelled for work and would bring back “strange and curious” toys, which she loved to prise apart and put together again, she says.
Dong now hopes to channel this ingenuity towards creating personalized medical technologies that can repair tissues, treat disease and monitor health. “The real opportunity is to create programmable hydrogel materials whose physical, mechanical and biological properties can be tailored to a particular tissue, patient and clinical need,” she says. — Sandy Ong
JAMES EILLS: Strong signals
The body’s conversion of molecules such as pyruvate, a naturally occurring metabolite, can be visualized with equipment including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners. This is because each metabolite’s chemical state emits a unique magnetic signal, providing a real-time readout of cellular metabolism. However, these signals are inherently weak because only a tiny fraction of atomic nuclei in such molecules align with the magnetic field emitted by even the most powerful scanners. For James Eills, head of the Hyperpolarization Methods Lab at the Jülich Research Centre in Germany, innovative hyperpolarization techniques are the most promising answer to enhance magnetic signals, one of the biggest challenges in MRI and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR).
Hyperpolarization forces the nuclear spins of atoms to point in the same direction, increasing the fraction of spins that are aligned with the magnetic field and making undetectable signals visible. “Using hyperpolarized pyruvate allows clinicians to monitor diseases better than conventional imaging,” says Eills.
Currently, in biomedical MRI imaging, before injecting a contrast reagent solution, clinicians hyperpolarize the molecules with a method called dissolution dynamic nuclear polarization. Although powerful, this method requires expensive machinery and needs long preparation times. For this reason, Eills believes that it is important to find better ways to hyperpolarize the molecules used as contrast reagents.
He has worked on this challenge since his undergraduate days at the University of Southampton, UK, in the early 2010s, pursuing it through master’s and PhD research at the University of California, Berkeley, and Southampton, and continuing during a postdoc at the Helmholtz Institute in Mainz, Germany, in 2018. He developed methods to try to improve the transfer of spin polarization from parahydrogen, a form of hydrogen gas in which the nuclear spins are aligned in opposite directions, to clinically relevant metabolites such as pyruvate and fumarate. Parahydrogen-induced polarization (PHIP) increases the magnetic resonance signal by several orders of magnitude while avoiding the complexity and cost of conventional dissolution dynamic methods. This work4, carried out through collaborations with researchers in the United States, United Kingdom, Italy and Germany, earned him and his colleagues the 2021 Erwin Schrödinger Prize to recognize outstanding collaborative research.
Nevertheless, there is a drawback in the PHIP method that Eills and his collaborators developed: it applies only to molecules that are amenable to the addition of hydrogen — a process called hydrogenation. “The challenge we face in my lab is to find new ways to induce PHIP,” he says. Such innovative ways to hyperpolarize molecules would widen the range of options available for biomedical imaging.
It is a quest that Eills has been pursuing since his second postdoc in 2021 at the Institute for Bioengineering of Catalonia in Barcelona, Spain, where he tackled another important bottleneck in the field. When using strong radio-frequency pulses to manipulate nuclear spins, the strength of the pulse can partially destroy the delicate quantum state of the nuclei. As a result, the tiny magnetic signals emitted by the manipulated nuclei can be lost. Eills and his collaborators attempted to solve this by introducing an atomic sensor to detect microscopic changes in local magnetic fields using laser light, rather than radio waves5.
Eills traces his passion for physical chemistry back to attending a 2011 lecture as a college student by the renowned British physical chemist, Peter Atkins. “What caught my attention was Professor Atkins describing the idea of negative temperature in a thermodynamic system,” remembers Eills. “Years later we create negative nuclear spin temperatures all the time using pulsed magnetic fields. What seemed impossible back then is now a simple trick to help us in our experiments.”
Every advance that Eills has brought to the field has helped to address a different obstacle in metabolic MRI applications. Although PHIP-derived imaging agents still need improvements in purity for clinical use, in a recent preprint6 Eills’s team showed their potential on human biopsy samples to measure drug response in real time. — Anna Napolitano

articles.title: Structural basis of ligand recognition and gating in mosquito IRs
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 14 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11239-3Structural basis of ligand recognition and gating in mosquito IRs
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Ionotropic receptors (IRs) are essential for insect olfaction, enabling the detection of carboxylic acids, amines, moisture, and temperature cues that mediate critical behaviors, including mosquito host-seeking 1,2.
However, the structural mechanisms underlying ligand specificity and channel activation in these receptors remain unclear.
Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures and functional validation of the IR8a-IR75k complex from the malaria mosquito Anopheles stephensi, a carboxylic acid detector, captured in four states: the ligand-free full-length closed form (apo state), the ligand induced full-length open state, and the nonanoic acid (NA)- and octanoic acid (OA)-bound extracellular domains.
These structures reveal a dynamic ligand-binding pocket in IR75k, in which specificity is determined by alkyl chain length and carboxylate geometry.
Ligand binding triggers closure of IR75k’s bilobed ligand binding domain (LBD), and this conformational change propagates through conserved mechanical linkers to the transmembrane domain (TMD), functioning as a molecular lever that dilates the pore via outward displacement of transmembrane helices.
This gating mechanism was further corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations and electrophysiology.
These insights provide an atomic resolution view of IR mediated host detection in mosquitoes and establish a foundation for the rational design of next generation mosquito control strategies targeting host-seeking behavior.

When people think of fat, they typically picture the jiggly tissue around the belly that stores extra calories. That’s white fat. But there’s another type, called brown fat, that does the opposite. Typically found around the neck, armpits and in the chest, brown fat burns calories to generate heat and has been linked to health benefits.
A study of more than 100,000 people — the largest of its kind — is now expanding that list of benefits. It revealed that people with ‘active’ brown fat are less affected by a number of health issues, including type 2 diabetes, depression and anxiety, than are those without it. Researchers used an artificial-intelligence model to quantify, from scans, the participants’ active brown fat, which is fat that is ‘turned on’ and burning calories. They concluded that the more active brown fat people have, the greater the protection they have from disorders and diseases.
“This is one of the most comprehensive and, probably, significant works in the field,” says Shingo Kajimura, a molecular biologist at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts.
Because this is a retrospective study, more work is needed to prove that brown fat is indeed causing all these benefits, says Irfan Lodhi, a molecular biologist at Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri. “But it’s still a very interesting and surprising study,” he says.
Turning up the heat
Scientists have known for decades that brown fat burns calories to produce heat. The fat helps newborns to stay warm, and scientists thought it vanished after babies developed the ability to shiver. But in 2009, researchers reported the discovery of brown fat in human adults for the first time2,3,4.
To map active brown fat in people, scientists use imaging techniques that highlight metabolically active tissue. They inject people with a type of radioactive glucose, and use a combination of positron emission tomography (PET) and computed tomography (CT) scans to reveal which tissues are taking up the glucose — highlighting where brown fat is activated.
These techniques are typically also used to diagnose and monitor cancer. So, a team led by Paul Cohen, a physician-scientist at the Rockefeller University in New York City, partnered with Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, also in New York, to obtain data from more than 100,000 people who had these scans while going through treatment there.

Wearable devices that can track health data offer a promising new research frontier, but a journal case study published in 2020 illustrates one of their core problems1.
The study describes a 70-year-old woman with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation — bouts of fast, irregular heartbeat that can be symptomatic or silent. This form of atrial fibrillation often resolves without treatment, but because of the patient’s other risk factors for stroke, her doctors put her on anticoagulant medication to lower the chance of a deadly blood clot.
The patient wore a smartwatch that included an app for monitoring heartbeat and generating electrocardiogram (ECG) readouts. In the year following her diagnosis, she checked those ECG readouts 916 times. She turned up to one consultation with her electrophysiologist — clinicians who specialize in arrhythmia — with a printed stack of those ECGs, according to Lindsey Rosman, who co-authored the paper describing the case.
“When I say stack, I mean hundreds,” says Rosman, a clinical health psychologist at Northwestern University in Chicago, Illinois.
This example illustrates the huge challenge that wearable devices — often not approved for medical use and now being worn by hundreds of millions of people globally — are posing in terms of the vast amount of data they produce. Patients, clinicians and researchers are increasingly having to make sense of this growing mountain of information, whether from approved or non-approved devices, without getting overwhelmed. But if this can be overcome, there are potentially groundbreaking applications for consumer devices, or clinically developed ‘medical-grade’ wearables, in diagnosing, managing or preventing heart conditions, neurological disorders and metabolic diseases.
Monitoring and managing
From the perspective of doctors who specialize in heart-rhythm disorders, devices such as smartwatches present an extraordinary technological opportunity. “For the first time, we could monitor our patients for long periods with inexpensive devices,” says Rod Passman, a cardiac electrophysiologist and director of the Center for Arrhythmia Research at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, Illinois.
That’s especially useful in atrial fibrillation, in which a chronic or worsening irregular heartbeat raises the risk that blood will pool in the left atrium and form a clot that can travel to the brain and cause a stroke. Around one in three people with atrial fibrillation will experience a stroke, so are put on blood-thinning medication for life. But anticoagulants come with side effects, including the risk of excessive bleeding.
Despite the variability in the severity of the condition, and the availability and use of other treatments and prevention, Passman says “we have this paradigm where if you have atrial fibrillation and other risk factors, you’re on a blood thinner for life, regardless of whether your episodes are once a day, once a year, or you’ve lost weight or had an ablation, and the atrial fibrillation is gone”.
Passman and colleagues are investigating whether it’s possible to use wearables to monitor the frequency of episodes and adjust treatment accordingly. In their REACT-AF trial, a multi-centre US-based trial run out of Northwestern University in Chicago, patients with atrial fibrillation are randomized either to stay on their usual dose of anticoagulants or to wear a smartwatch with an app that will alert them when they need to restart medication temporarily. Many smartwatches can already measure heart rate, either with photoplethysmography — which uses light to detect changes in blood volume — or electrocardiography, a simple version of the ECG monitors used in clinical settings. The innovation here is the app that interprets those signals.
“We expect to show that this strategy is equally effective at preventing stroke,” Passman says. “But because patients are on blood thinners a fraction of the time, they will have less bleeding, they’ll pay less for medication, and we expect an improvement in life quality.”
There’s interest in whether wearable devices could be used to screen for and predict undiagnosed heart arrhythmias, including rare ones linked to sudden arrhythmic death syndrome. Each year, in the United States, around 4,000 children and young adults die from a heart arrhythmia. Sudden arrhythmic death syndrome is caused by a range of often inherited disorders, many of which are asymptomatic. In many cases, the first warning is also the last.
One review2 found evidence that consumer smartwatches could detect a range of arrhythmias beyond atrial fibrillation, but warned of the risk of false positives due to inaccurate readings. Smartwatches aren’t being used routinely to identify at-risk patients because they haven’t been shown to be effective, Passman says. But with millions of people wearing the devices, the medical potential is clear.
Although doctors and researchers are more cautious with the idea of using standard consumer smartwatches as a screening and diagnostic tool, consumers have fewer hesitations. Rosman says patients are increasingly sending smartwatch readouts about their heart, stress levels or even sleep patterns to their doctor via patient portals, bringing them along to consultations, or rushing to the emergency department because of an alert from their device.
Sometimes wearable devices do turn up something useful. Passman says patients have received a diagnosis of an arrhythmia because their smart device alerted them that something was wrong. But that doesn’t necessarily translate into better health outcomes. “While it makes intuitive sense that that would be a great thing to do because we’d find atrial fibrillation early — we would get patients on blood thinners and prevent strokes — we’ve yet to prove that’s the case,” he says.
The three-year Heartline study3, funded by Apple and pharmaceutical company Janssen, aims to do that. US researchers are recruiting around 28,000 people across the country aged 65 or older — some with atrial fibrillation, and some without — to see whether early detection or monitoring of symptoms using an Apple Watch improves cardiovascular outcomes.
Another arena where the ubiquity of wearable devices is opening up a new paradigm of management and treatment is in neurology. Consumer smartwatches are already widely used for the detection of falls, which can result from frailty or neurological conditions; one controlled trial in 22 healthy adults4 found that they correctly identified 77% of falls with a false-positive rate of 1.7%. But there’s growing interest in their application for monitoring and alerting wearers or their carers to seizures.
“Seizures are traditionally reported based on others witnessing the event,” says paediatric neurologist Anup Patel, from Nationwide Children’s Hospital in Columbus, Ohio. People who are alone at the time of their seizure might be unaware they have had one.
There are a small number of specialized regulator-approved seizure-detection wearable devices available in the United States and Europe. Patel says these approved devices, which can include arm bands and patches, are increasingly being used in clinical trials to provide more accurate information. But he has concerns about the accuracy of detection, suggesting that the algorithms on approved medical devices — which analyse movement, temperature and heart rate — might only be around 90% accurate, with a risk of false-positive alerts. In his experience, families often start using a seizure-alert device, but stop because of the false positives.
Another barrier to more widespread use of such seizure-monitoring devices is that they are more obviously a medical device, not a familiar consumer device such as a smartwatch, and that could attract stigma and attention. So patients might prefer consumer devices if they can provide the same service.
Another scenario that is generating a lot of interest is whether wearable consumer devices such as smartwatches could be used to flag an impending seizure so people can get to a safe position, or take medication that could prevent or mitigate an attack. “Are there biometric parameters that can help to say, ‘When X, Y, Z happens, you’re going to have a seizure’,” Patel says.
This isn’t unique to epilepsy; there could be a range of scenarios in neurology, or even across the spectrum of disease, in which a wearable device could warn wearers if they are at higher risk of some kind of adverse event; a migraine, for example. “Are there parameters that we can have ahead of time to say, ‘You’re at risk for a fall,’ or ‘Today’s a bad day to go out, you may want to take it easy’?” he says.
With all of these potential uses for wearables, a key issue is how they can be integrated into health-care systems to make a difference at a population level. Clinicians have the expertise to handle the wealth of information that devices produce, but they’re in a bind: what is their responsibility when it comes to unregulated data from an unapproved device sent to them outside hours by a worried patient?
Patel says that early on, there was a concern that doctors might face litigation if they didn’t review these data promptly and a patient then experienced an adverse health event. “Largely, that fear has been relieved because it’s not the case, and there are clear parameters that say no, you are not liable for that,” he says.
